speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) invited me to comment on the situation arising out of the withdrawal of the United States and British offers of financial help to Egypt in connection with the Aswan high dam project and asked whether I would instruct the Canadian executive director of the international bank to press that institution to finance the project notwithstanding this change in the situation.
I am sure that the house will agree that the offer of aid by one country for a particular project in another country or the withdrawal of such an offer are not matters on which it would be appropriate for me to comment. It may, however, be useful to the house if I recall some of the main facts connected with the role of the international bank in the Aswan high dam project.
The project itself is a very ambitious one consisting of three main elements: First, the construction at Aswan of a dam 400 feet high and three miles long to store the waters of the Nile; second, the use of the stored water to extend perennial irrigation to some two million acres of land, which would raise by one-third the amount of irrigated land in Egypt; and third, the installation of hydroelectric production and distributive systems of a capacity which would more than double the hydroelectric power available to Egypt. The estimated cost of the project and ancillary works is $1,350 million, of which $400 million is represented by private investment, leaving $950 million to be publicly financed. Of this $400 million is represented by foreign exchange requirements and the balance of $550 million by local expenditures on goods and services.
Mr. Eugene Black, the president of the international bank, and members of his staff have been engaged in discussions with the Egyptian authorities and studies of this important and complicated project during the past two or three years. At the end of 1955, Mr. Black indicated that, given the existence of certain conditions, he would be prepared to recommend to the bank's board of executive directors a loan or loans to Egypt for the Aswan high dam. After a careful study of Egypt's economic prospects, the management of the bank concluded that the maximum external debt which the Egyptian economy could be expected to service in respect of the project would be of the order of half the foreign exchange costs, or approximately $200 million. Accordingly, if the project was to be
TMr. Pearson.]

executed without prejudice to the Egyptian economy, it would be necessary for the Egyptian government to find elsewhere the remainder of the needed foreign exchange without imposing additional debt charges on the economy.
The house will be aware that the governments of the United States and United Kingdom had indicated their willingness to provide together on a grant basis some $70 million toward the foreign exchange cost of the first stages of the project and that they would be prepared at a later date, in the light of the then existing circumstances and subject to legislative authority, to give sympathetic consideration to financing the later stages of the project as a supplement to bank lending.
With the withdrawal of United States and United Kingdom offers of assistance, it would appear that the availability of the total foreign exchange requirements of the project on a basis which will not unduly encumber the Egyptian economy can no longer be regarded as assured.
The international bank has issued no statement with regard to this matter. I would not wish to suggest that with regard to any particular project the management of the bank should depart from the normal lending criteria which have been established not only in the interests of the bank itself but of the borrowers. I think the house can be certain that if at some future time a proposal for a bank loan for the Aswan project comes before the executive directors of the bank it will be given careful and sympathetic consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now dealing with the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) that Bill No. 442 be read the second time. In reference to the entire proposal of the dominion government as contained in the bill, our position was stated by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) at the resolution stage on July 16. That resolution was passed on division. The house is now asked to carry into legislative form and effect the formula which was the essence of the federal government's proposals. We are asked to do so with full knowledge that no provincial government has yet given its approval to those proposals and indeed with full knowledge that there has been widespread disapproval of the government's proposals on the ground of their inadequacy. I therefore say, Mr. Speaker, that the effect of reading this bill the second time would be, as I understand it, to give effect to a principle that the formula contained in the bill is adequate and ought to be adopted.
The question that we ought to ask ourselves is similar to that which my leader put before the house when he spoke a week ago. To paraphrase it, I would say the question before us is whether or not at this time there is evidence that the proposals of the government, and in particular this formula, will satisfactorily meet the demands which are actually now imposed upon provincial governments, municipal councils and boards of education throughout Canada and particularly whether they will be adequate over the five-year period during which the new scheme is intended to be in effect.
I point out at the outset, sir, that this is enabling legislation. If it is adopted, it will vest very wide powers in the Minister of Finance, and the powers vested in him include the power to legislate in the form of regulations.
As to the details of the formula, suffice it to say at this point that it is an actuarial maze to most people. The formula itself would undoubtedly confuse most citizens. Talk of tax equalization payments, provincial revenue stabilization payments, tax rental agreements, gross national product, average personal income, and other expressions in which this formula abounds make it very difficult for the average citizen to appreciate

Indeed, it would be interesting, particularly in the light of the fact that no Liberal member spoke on the resolution, except the Minister of Finance, to put some of them to a test on the grasp of the details of this formula which they are now asked to approve. Every citizen, however, is interested in the result.
I propose to look at this formula in terms of the results that will follow from its adoption in legislative form. Surely, that is a fair test. Let us then put the new proposed formula in its proper perspective. It is estimated by the government that it would make available to the provinces in return for certain forms of revenue now constitutionally open to the provinces to collect on their own behalf a total this year of $653 million, which represents an increase of $115 million or 20 per cent over the sums that would have been paid to all provinces under the type of agreement now in effect if all the provinces were parties to it this year. It is evident at once that, so far as the provinces themselves are concerned, the new formula, in relation to the scheme which has been in effect for the past nine years, does represent an improvement. It is better. But, sir, we must go farther and ask ourselves if it is good enough, good enough today and good enough to be carried into legislative effect for the full period of five years commencing in the spring of 1957.
The problem, as everyone knows, arises from the fact that there are certain fields of taxation which under our constitutional division of responsibilities are common to both the dominion and provincial fields. If we look at the constitution with regard for the history of the intervening 89 years we must recognize at once, as fairminded men and women, that the provinces in these common fields of taxation have at least equal rights with the dominion.
Indeed, there have been times when it was argued that, because the provincial authorities were confined to taxation in its direct form, there was a constitutional priority created in their favour in that field. But at any rate, sir, whatever may be the validity of that argument, it is undeniable that constitutionally the provinces have at least an equal right and an equal status with the dominion in the fields of direct taxation.
Historically the provinces have claimed a priority because they were the first to occupy those fields.

As I said, having dealt with the position taken in public statements by the provincial premiers, I come now to ask the question, is the attitude that the provincial premiers have taken reasonable? We have to ask ourselves the question, in weighing this issue, whether

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements we are entitled to overlook the position taken by these provincial premiers and blandly and blindly legislate this formula into statutory effect.
Let no one underestimate the importance of the provinces and municipalities in the field of government of this country. They are the governments that are closest to the people. Anyone who has had experience of municipal government and has entered the federal field is well aware of the fact that is the form of government that is closest to the people. It is a form of government much older than our federal form of government in this country.
Today Canada is facing a period of very rapid development. We have talked freely in this house about the rapidity of the development of resources in this country today. The development of all the resources of this country except those in the territories is constitutionally vested in the provincial jurisdiction, and it is relatively little help that the provinces are receiving from the federal government in the form of conservation of resources or other forms.
New enterprises are created by individual effort and initiative, and then what happens? What is the result on governmental responsibilities and revenues? Let us take an example or two. When a new mine is opened up and development begins, the first thing that is called for is the construction of roads into the mine and the provision of the other services which in unorganized portions of the province are the responsibility of the provincial government. Then, when staff comes in and the little community is established, what is the form of government that then must assume the burdens? It is the municipal form of government. The demand at once is made for the construction of streets, and the provision of schools, police and fire protection, health and welfare services and municipal administration. The cost of every one of these municipal services, all of which are demanded by the people, is rising in astronomical proportions at all times.
But what is the government that derives the first revenue from this new enterprise? I say to you, sir, it is the federal government. The first time a pay cheque is given by that enterprise to an employee, the federal government steps in to receive its first cut on the first pay cheque.
The figures that I ascribed to Premier Smallwood in the extract that I read from his statement indicate the tremendous benefit that the federal government derives in respect of revenues from the development of new enterprises. But it is only at a later stage that the municipal and provincial governments begin to derive their revenue benefits.

In the meantime the burden of providing the services that are required in that particular municipality falls on the municipal government and also on the provincial government.
Take another example: the construction of a new industry in a town or a city. On whom does the burden fall of providing the services that are required for such an industry and for the employees of that industry? It is the municipal government. The first burden falls on the municipality. But what level of government derives the first revenue benefit? Again it is the federal government. Out of the first pay cheque comes the federal cut.
There is a situation which must be recognized and, in my respectful submission, has not been recognized by the federal government in its relations with the provincial premiers. Sir, Mr. Harvey Perry, director of the Canadian Tax Foundation, has summed that situation up in these words:
Given peace and prosperity the provinces and municipalities will henceforth bear the brunt of the cost of providing expanded government services and facilities for a rapidly growing country, whereas their revenue sources, being less elastic, will rise more slowly than those of the federal government. It is also becoming clear that barring war and depression the relative needs of the federal government for revenue to support functions in its own sphere will decline in the foreseeable future whereas the federal treasury is the one that will reap the greatest share of the benefit from an expanding economy.
If you want any further example of what an increase in population in an expanding municipality means, just take the experience of the city of Edmonton. In the brief it recently submitted to the Gordon royal commission it gave the estimate that if an increase of 175,000 takes place in the city's population over the next quarter century it will be necessary to construct 500 miles of streets and sidewalks and 450 miles of sewers and water mains and to connect 180,000 utility services of all kinds. The brief pointed out that 1,100 schoolrooms and 3,200 hospital beds will have to be provided for this increase in the population. The brief concluded:
Such a program suggests expenditures in the nature of $300 million over the next 25 years for schools, hospitals and general capital requirements.
Sir, statements of that kind are entitled to be taken with the greatest gravity. When there is talk about "rich provinces" people usually think in terms of the stage of development that a province has reached in regard to its resources, but here in a debate of this kind what we must concern ourselves with is the burden cast on all such provinces as well as those that are not classed in that category, the burdens that are increasing so rapidly with the pace of development of resources.

A word now about the outlook of the provinces and municipalities in relation to their revenues and fiscal future. The proportion of the tax dollar that is going to the three levels of government is always a fruitful source for study. In 1939 the dominion collected 47 cents out of the total tax dollar in this country. In 1955 it collected 68 cents. In 1939 the provinces collected 23 cents out of the Canadian tax dollar, and in 1955 the provinces combined collected only 17 cents of that dollar.

In 1939 the municipalities' share of the tax dollar was 31 cents. In 1955 it was only 15 cents out of that tax dollar.
What of the burdens of the municipalities and the provinces all this time? Current expenditures of provincial governments have increased very substantially in the post-war period. Total current expenditure, excluding provision for tax repayment, increased from $402 million in the fiscal year 1946-47 to $1,261 million in the fiscal year 1955-56. Almost every category of provincial expenditure has greatly increased. Between the fiscal years 1946 and 1955 total current expenditure of provincial governments increased 98-6 per cent, while Canada's population increased only by 26-9 per cent. Highway expenditures increased 154-9 per cent. Public welfare and relief expenditures increased 123-8 per cent, and education 102-8 per cent. In other words, sir, the provinces are being called upon today to provide services which are thrice as expensive as the services provided in 1946.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration asked for some enlightenment on the position of the province of Newfoundland. Well, I am glad to give him that needed information. In the brief it submitted to the Gordon royal commission the government of Newfoundland stated that its road program would necessitate an expenditure of at least $5 million annually on capital account, that water and sewerage systems would involve $1 million annually, and schools and hospitals at
23, 1956	6293
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements least $1,500,000 each year for the next 25 years. The brief went on to stress how much below the general level of services those of the province of Newfoundland are compared with those prevailing in other provinces. In discussing the financing of necessary expenditures the brief concluded that the province's "ability to provide the means both for overcoming the present deficiency in social capital and meeting the requirements of prospective growth is very limited." Then the province asked the federal government for substantially increased grants for highway construction and other purposes.
What of the position of the provinces and municipalities in regard to capital expenditure, because every member of the house knows that necessary capital expenditures were deferred during the war by provinces and municipalities and that a tremendous backlog had accumulated by the beginning of the post-war period? The trend in post-war capital spending by both provincial and municipal governments has been sharply upward. In 1946 total capital expenditures of provincial and municipal governments and their agencies amounted to $276 million, representing an increase of more than 80 per cent over the previous year. Since that time every province's capital expenditures have increased many times over, from $138 million in 1946 to $677 million in 1955. Municipal capital expenditures, although rising somewhat less than those of provincial governments, had increased by 1955 to more than four times the 1946 level, from $138 million in the earlier year to $546 million in 1955. While it may not be possible for the provincial and municipal authorities to carry out their total planned capital spending for 1956, there can be little doubt that these expenditures will be higher than in 1955. Provincial governments and their agencies have announced the intention of spending $941 million on capital account in 1956, and municipal governments $603 million.
I turn now to current municipal expenditures. Here we will see that on current expenditure the burden on the municipalities rose from $348 million in 1946 to $873 million in 1955. In the latter year education accounted for 32 [DOT] 7 per cent of the total, general administration, including police and fire protection, 31 per cent, public welfare 14-5 per cent, highways, roads and streets 14-7 per cent, and debt charges, excluding debt repayment, 7-1 per cent.
Every hon. member here knows well the situation with respect to his own municipality. I intend to mention only three in particular before passing on to another subject. In its brief to the Gordon royal commission the city of Montreal, Canada's most populous city,

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements stated that the volume of municipal investment presently necessary, and which the city considers should already have been undertaken to make up deficiencies accumulated since 1934, totals $503,300,000. Included in this huge sum are waterworks, $40,300,000; collector sewers, $33 million; local improvements, $17,500,000; parks and playgrounds, $40 million. A substantial part of the total backlog involves expenditures necessary to relieve traffic bottlenecks in the city: expressways, $147 million; subway, $87 million; parking, $10 million; tunnels or bridges to the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, $60 million.
Or look at the city of Quebec, Mr. Speaker. In its brief to the Gordon royal commission it said:
Whereas our budget is $12,700,000, including school costs, some cities with approximately the same population (225,000) have at their disposal a budget varying between $15 million and $20 million. As you can see, the margin is a substantial one. The present situation leaves us no alternative but to reduce expenditures more and more, while putting off urgent works until a later date. We cannot act otherwise under the present circumstances without further weakening the financial structure of our city and the economic well-being of its citizens.
The last example I have taken is the city of Halifax which in its brief expressed grave fears that it would be unable to raise the required revenue in future years because of its limited real property tax base. Other municipalities submitted briefs to the same effect, my own city of Toronto among them, drawing attention to the prodigious burden laid upon the metropolitan area by the need for providing new school facilities, new transportation, water, sewerage and other new works required.
Mr. Speaker, education must have a special word of mention because education affects all the municipalities across the country and is today faced with a situation that can only properly be described as critical. As a result of increase in the birth rate and increase in immigration the school population has been rapidly enlarged. The cost of providing school facilities becomes greater all the time. The pressure on existing school facilities has now become so acute that in many schools the facilities are admittedly hopelessly inadequate, either in point of quality or physical extent, to provide for the growing school population. In many schools the children are simply being taken in relays, with all the strains that this imposes on staff and upon administrative machinery and all facilities.
The Minister of Finance and the government have been often urged in this house to recognize the fact that the sources of revenue open to the municipalities and to the


provinces are inadequate to provide for the expanding cost of education, as things stand today. In approaching this present renewal of fiscal arrangements between the dominion and the provinces, the Minister of Finance had a golden opportunity to recognize that inescapable fact and to do something to meet it; but, Mr. Speaker, as things stand at the moment, he has thrown away that opportunity. The increase that is offered in the new formula over the amount provided by the existing agreements cannot be pretended by anyone to meet the needs of the provinces and of the municipalities in relation to education. There is in this country no governmental function more important than education. The benefits of education are not confined locally in the municipality or even the province. For example those excellent universities in the maritime provinces which are educating so many in proportion to the population there are doing so not just for the benefit of the maritime provinces. The benefits of the excellent university education available in the maritimes are transmitted throughout the whole of this country as the graduates go elsewhere, as do many of them.
Student enrolment is bound to increase in this country by leaps and bounds at all levels of our educational system. University enrolment in Canada is expected to rise from
66.000	to somewhere between 110,600 and 135,200 by the fall of 1964. In Ontario it will jump from 20,400 last year to 42,700 in the same period. The median of the all-Canada projection is 123,000, an increase of
57.000	over the present, and that is just by the year 1964. In Ontario alone the increase will be 22,000; that is, 40 per cent of the Canadian increase will occur in the province of Ontario.
By and large, I think the provinces have done all they can to assist the municipalities. Indeed, in his comment of July 18, Premier Frost had this to say:
Education in its primary, secondary, vocational and university phases has added immense burdens, and we have by no means even begun to feel the full weight of the problem. As a province we are not static and our problems continue to grow. Today we have a school population in primary and secondary schools of approximately one million. This population has been built up since the beginning of this province. But the next 10 years alone will see 750,000 children added to this enrolment.
That is an increase of 75 per cent in the next ten-year period. It is a staggering increase and the cost of providing educational facilities for that staggering increase in the school population will be literally colossal. I am sure I do not need to detain the house with more figures in this field.

The plight of the municipalities is desperate. I think the provinces have done all that lies within their power to help the municipalities. In Ontario grants to the municipalities in the last twelve years have risen from $18 million to $185 millions and 45 per cent of all provincial government revenue now goes to the municipalities from the provincial treasury. But it remains a fact that 84 per cent of all municipal revenue comes from the direct levy on real estate which has now become virtually a capital levy and is crushing in the burden it casts upon the home owner.
Mr. Speaker, I leave this subject with this observation. Provincial burdens are bound to increase. Municipal burdens are bound to increase. One could cite many examples of that fact.
I now wish to say a word-and I shall not be long-about the attitude of the dominion government. During the war practically everybody accepted the necessity of centralization. It was done to meet a crisis and legislative jurisdiction was concentrated at Ottawa to an unprecedented degree. Similarly, the tax-collecting functions of government were concentrated to an unparalleled extent here at Ottawa. But much of the mentality that pervaded the federal government's thinking in those war years has been carried into the years of peace. I should be the first to concede that the federal government has assumed increased burdens in this post-war period. But I do say that this increased burden which the federal government is wont to parade has not been commensurate with the increase in its revenues from these common sources of taxation. The camel got its head into the tent, and instead of being content to share the tent with the former occupant has been busy trying to push the camel driver out.
In the present measure, the extent to which the federal government will permit the occupation of these joint fields by the provinces with the dominion, without the unhappy incident of double taxation, is just 9 percentage points out of 47 percentage points that the federal government levies on the taxable income of corporations and just 10 per cent out of the levy on personal income tax and one-half of the succession duties. The way in which the federal government has proceeded through this take-it-or-leave-it attitude indicates they are now proceeding to the next stage in their tactics of divide and conquer. They applied that method in 1946 and 1947 and later, first of all on the provinces with weaker fiscal positions. Their approach, if they repeat these tactics of divide and conquer, in that way will be inimical to

What needs to be done at the outset as a preliminary necessity is that the federal government should recognize the constitutional position of the provinces, but they have not shown a disposition to do so. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who does not seem to be listened to any more by hon. members opposite, long ago drew attention to the dangers of separating the responsibilities of tax collection from tax expenditure. He said that would always lead to extravagance. The late Mr. Mackenzie King, in 1945, had something similar to say to those hon. members opposite who have not completely forgotten him. He said:
There will, however, be no solution of existing problems which involve financial outlays so long as one government or agency is the taxing agency and another government or agency is the spending agency. In other words we must return as regards our revenues and expenditures as in all else to responsible government in the fullest meaning of that term, whereby the governments that spend public moneys must be the governments which through the agency of taxation raise what is to be spent.

Now, sir, I come to this concluding observation. I think this formula ought to be judged by the results which it will create. The provisions that will accrue to the provinces from the three features of the formula are inadequate. A new conference between the federal arid provincial governments is altogether desirable, if the federal government will not go to such a conference with the same attitude as it went to the conference in 1955 and 1956. There is no use, of course, in having a conference if the federal government is simply going to continue to take this rigid, inflexible, take-it-or-leave-it attitude. On the other hand, if the federal government will give adequate recognition to the constitutional position and the needs of the provinces, and will genuinely seek an understanding to meet their needs, then a new conference should be called.
There is no use, so far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition is concerned, asking us to approve a form of dominion-provincial fiscal arrangement which has not received the approval of a single provincial government. If there could be, on the part of the federal government, a change of attitude, and after that change in attitude they will call a new conference, then fruitful results I am certain could be achieved. It would necessitate a fall session of parliament. We would be quite happy to see a fall session in order to achieve this praiseworthy object. We realize that these agreements are going to run out at the end of the present fiscal year, March 31, 1957 and therefore the legislation, to allow adequate planning by all governments concerned, must be passed this year, 1956. We are quite prepared, if the federal government will follow the course we have urged, to come back if necessary for a fall session. But we say that the provision made by this measure for the provinces is inadequate.
If hon. members opposite ask me what our position is I can say to them that we would do more for the provinces than the federal government has shown it is willing to do in this measure. We believe the federal government can do more and can afford to do more.
Let there be no question about our position in reference to other features of this matter of federal-provincial fiscal relations. We recognize completely the principle of equalization grants, sharing the revenues which if the federal government were not in this field would accrue simply to the provinces. We recognize the claim of the provinces in a weaker financial position; we certainly do. So far as we are concerned that recognition' is axiomatic, basic and fundamental in our approach to this subject.


We look upon provinces like the maritimes, which have not the hinterland territory and undeveloped resources, broadly speaking, that are available to most of the other provinces. We say that account must be taken of those differences in the prospects for future development. Those provinces such as the maritimes-and I am not confining this to the maritimes-in a weaker financial position have been neglected by this government far too long.
I say again the provisions made by this formula, which is the only one that this government is prepared to put forward or agree to, will result in either double taxation, the imposition of new or increased sales taxes, bankruptcy or stagnation or, as the former premier of Nova Scotia warned, in a unitary state. So far as we of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition are concerned, sir, we do not wish to see any of these things happen. We believe we have ample warnings from competent provincial sources of the dangers of these results flowing from a continuance of the adamantine attitude of the government opposite in these matters. Benefit will accrue, as it always has accrued, to the dominion' and to the federal treasury from strong provincial fiscal positions.
If hon. members are to be told now that the way for the provinces to meet their crushing needs is to go out and levy additional taxes in these fields of direct taxation and in that way create double taxation, I remind hon. members that it is the same taxpayer who will be paying these increased taxes and the plight of the taxpayer in his aggregate burdens is something concerning which we have reminded this government on more than one occasion.
The Minister of Finance knows that he is headed for a huge surplus in this fiscal year; that surplus may run from half a billion dollars to a larger figure, if the government does not dissipate it in extravagance or if it does not hide it, as it has done in other years, by putting great sums of money into various pockets of the government exchequer.
The government apparently has decided that it prefers that the provinces and the municipalities be starved, that they should be compelled to remain in a financial strait-jacket, in order that the federal government may put on a grandstand show next spring and use tax reductions following this enormous budget surplus as election bait.

Mr. Speaker, on every occasion when bills are introduced in this House of Commons, it happens that some hon. member will say- and rightly so-that it is an important bill, or perhaps that it is the most important bill to be presented to the house in the course of that session.
As far as I am concerned, Bill No. 442 which we are now discussing on second reading is without doubt the most important bill that can possibly come before this house at this session.
This provides us with the opportunity of what we might term a five-year review of the responsibility of the governments and the financial possibilities of the three realms of government in this country meeting their responsibilities, because Bill 442 gives the power of signing new five-year agreements concerning financial arrangements. It is the time for very serious consideration and review of the situation as it exists governmentally and financially in this country. Because of the importance of these things, this bill is one that should not be discussed with high flights of eloquence or emotionalism but rather it should be discussed in as calm and dispassionate a manner as is humanly possible.
6298	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements I take the position that there are two fundamental facts we have to keep in mind in considering this bill and all that it means. First of all we must remember that many years ago the fathers of confederation laid down the terms of union. I am convinced that no one of any party or of any sense will criticize the sincerity, integrity and brilliance of the fathers of confederation. They laid down what in effect is the fundamental constitution of this country and the jurisdiction and constitutional rights. I think I am safe in saying that at this time no one would contemplate any revision of the British North America Act which would in any way interfere with, change or abrogate the constitutional rights of the governments of this country. However, as men change and as times change we have to recognize that even with all their brilliance, even paying them the highest compliment for the remarkable job they did, at the time of confederation there could not possibly or conceivably have been any idea of the progress and development which would occur in this country and the changing responsibilities of government. That is something which could not have been conceived so many years ago.
Therefore, those of us who are now members of the House of Commons, I feel, have the responsibility of recognizing the basic principles and precepts, of recognizing the correctness of the jurisdiction and constitutional rights, and we should at this time endeavour when we consider a bill which lays the foundations for a new five-year contract to analyse the situation as it is and to see if we can devise a fiscal policy which will enable all governments to meet their new and growing responsibilities.
I said that there were two basic considerations which we had to keep in mind, and the second is that each one of us loves the province in which he resides and the constituency which he represents. Some of us live in provinces which are wealthier than others and we want to see the best that is possible in our own constituency and our own province, but I am afraid that in discussing a matter of this nature too often we consider it from the provincial and not from the national point of view. I say that as one who has some knowledge of that attitude because I spent 20 years in a provincial legislature.
Mr. Speaker, the lights are out, but hon. members need not worry about that, because I am giving them the light in the sense it is required.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, I want to dissociate myself completely from the rumours that are now flying around the corridors of the parliament buildings. I do not believe that the Minister of Finance has taken a page out of the book of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by putting out the lights brought in a new system of closure. The lights went out at 12.45. If my memory is correct, when the war started in 1914, Earl Grey looked out of the windows of the foreign office in Great Britain and said, "The lights are going out over Europe." It may seem a strange analogy, but I want to say that in my estimation the Minister of Finance at this time, in the introduction of Bill 442, had the opportunity of putting on the lights for the Canadian nation by a new alignment of fiscal policy. I am sorry that he failed to throw the switch.
At the time of adjournment, I was pointing out that, although we recognize the thinking of provincial governments, and of citizens in provinces, for the maintenance of their own standards and the utilization of the benefits of their own resources, I thought-and I definitely do-that if we are real citizens we have to recognize that Canada as a nation can only be built up by a national attitude and not a parochial one.
The hon. member for Eglinton, in his one-hour talk this morning gave us the general views of himself and the party for whom he spoke. He concluded his remarks by stating that there were ten reasons why the official opposition was not going to support the second reading of this bill. I realize that it is a general practice to make one's remarks and conclude with points of a specific nature, but I am going to reverse the procedure. I am going to begin with ten points and then deal in general with them later. In doing so we would like to make this point very clear; that is, that the development of Canada and the status of all citizens in Canada is dependent upon our being a nation and not a series of parochial provinces.
This is based upon something which I think should be axiomatic, that Canada is not built up as a nation by the wealth of one, two or three provinces, by the industries in certain sections or by the activity of individuals in certain areas. The national wealth and well-being of Canada is the work of every solitary individual in the Dominion of Canada. It means that, irrespective of our position in various provinces, the work of the pioneers in the far outskirts of Canada, the work of those of what have been referred

to as the poor provinces of Canada, make up the national well-being of Canada. It very definitely is the feeling of this group, for whom I am speaking at the present time, that therefore every citizen of Canada is entitled to the best that can be given to him, irrespective of the province or part in which he lives, be it in a city or in a pioneering outskirt of our country.
With that being understood, as I have said, I am going to reverse the procedure of the hon. member for Eglinton. I am going to lay down ten points first and speak to them generally afterwards. I can assure you that our group has given very serious consideration to Bill No. 442. We believe that the following factors deserve the attention of the government and deserve the consideration of the members of this house on the second reading and at the committee stage of this bill:
1.	The C.C.F. group in this house is of the opinion that it is both advisable and necessary in the Canadian interests to continue dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements relative to income tax, corporation tax and succession duties.
2.	It was found necessary for the federal government in time of war, in the national interest, to ask for a dominion-provincial agreement, and in our opinion it is just as necessary to retain the policy in time of peace, whether it be under an expanding economy or with the possibility of a recession.
3.	Our federal group deplores the policy change of the federal government in that their latest proposals constitute a retreat from the basic principles and would appear to indicate a desire of the government to recede from an over-all taxation plan that prevents dual taxation and gives to the federal government a greater supervision of and influence upon the Canadian economy.
4.	The government proposals fail to recognize the fiscal needs of the provinces.
5.	Under the three plans submitted by the federal government there is no real incentive to the provinces to sign a tax rental agreement as there is no benefit accruing to those that come in as compared with those that stay out.
6.	Any dominion-provincial fiscal arrangement must recognize the increasing responsibilities that provincial and municipal governments have without the taxation power to finance the same.
7.	A municipality being the child of the provincial government, an understanding must be reached between the dominion and provincial authorities that a degree of benefits granted by the dominion, perhaps outside

the taxation agreement, to a fair extent be passed on by the provincial government to the municipal governments.
8.	Any dominion-provincial taxation agreement must include as part of the contract, or by declaration of government policy-and I emphasize that-the assumption of a degree of federal financial responsibility in the fields which constitutionally are the responsibility of provincial governments or municipalities, but the cost of which is beyond their taxation abilities.
9.	Without change in the provisions of the British North America Act, and recognizing the responsibilities and jurisdictions of provincial and municipal governments, the federal government in outlining the tax rental proposals must include therewith financial aid in the field of education, highway construction and capital participation in resources conservation and development as being for the general good of Canada.
Finally, No. 10. Although Canada anticipates an expanding economy, the dominion authorities agree to plan, in conjunction with the provincial and municipal governments, for joint financial participation in necessary works that can be undertaken in time of recession; and further agree to make available to municipal authorities low interest loans to enable them to meet the commitments required because of industrial development and population increase for which the municipalities must make a heavy capital investment for services and the federal government receives the greatest taxation gain.
The C.C.F. group in the House of Commons put those ten points forward as being the important factors that should be considered in discussion on second reading and in the committee stage of Bill No. 442. I said, sir, that after outlining these ten points I would speak in the time available on the general aspects in support of the same. When the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), spoke at the resolution stage he reminded the house and the government of the contention of the government of the day when the first proposals were made for a dominion-provincial taxation agreement in the three fields that are under discussion. The statement is of such importance that I want to repeat it. The statement of the federal government with respect to the proposals outlined in the green book in 1945 was:
To do these things fully and without destroying the federal system, the dominion government considers that it should have full and exclusive freedom to tax personal and corporate income and estates so that the restrictive effects of double and competitive taxation may be avoided and so that income earned and wealth accumulated nationally

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements can be fully and efficiently taxed for national purposes and the mutual advantage of all provinces.
Sir, that was an important statement. It is one that I personally agree with completely. Because of the exigencies of war it was found necessary by the federal government to operate as a nation, and they required not only certain controls but the over-all supervision of the national economy if we were to wage a successful war. All the provinces agreed. But, Mr. Speaker, we want to say this very definitely, that it is just as important for Canada to win the peace as it was for Canada to win the war. I know that can be called a trite statement but it is not. Having been blessed with the resources we have and having in mind the capabilities of our people, we should see to it that there is a reasonable standard of living and degree of prosperity for all the people of Canada, not just those in the wealthy provinces. Winning the peace means the development of Canada by applying the abilities, policies and national direction which we employed in winning the war in order to bring about the greatest good for all the people of this country.
In the event of a recession, and nobody knows whether or not we may encounter another one, it cannot be controlled by any province but only by the national government. We feel strongly that the powers and supervision that enabled Canada to play the wonderful part it did in the winning of the war should also be applied to the winning of the peace.
This, of course, takes me back to my opening remarks as to the responsibilities of various governments. The jurisdictions and constitutional rights are laid down by the British North America Act but the responsibilities have increased to an extent not known when confederation took place. It is regrettable that the present bill does not take into consideration the realities of the situation.
At the resolution stage a member placed the facts on the record with regard to the expenditures of government. In case they have been forgotten I should like to do so again. According to the government's own figures federal government expenditure from 1945 to 1955 increased from $4J billion to $4| billion, or 5-5 per cent. Provincial government expenditures increased from $384 million to $1J billion or 291-9 per cent, and the costs of municipal government went up by 276 per cent.
As pointed out by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) this morning, the municipalities and the provinces have had to make terrific capital expenditures. This, sir, has resulted in an amazing situation because

in the proceedings at the last dominion-provincial conference we find this:
It is noteworthy that, in these post-war years of prosperity, the indebtedness of the provinces, municipalities and their agencies has risen from $2-977 billion in 1945 to $5-715 billion in 1953, an increase of 92 per cent, while the federal government debt has actually been reduced from $18-438 billion to $18-276 billion.
It should not be necessary to emphasize the practical implications of these figures. Undoubtedly at the time of confederation it was thought that fiscal policies could be arranged on the basis of increase of population. That no longer applies today. One of the greatest needs in realigning fiscal policies with governmental responsibilities is a recognition of the fiscal needs of the provinces and their children, the municipalities. I think we must also have a recognition of the fact that the revenues of the federal government are dependent entirely on the prosperity of the provinces. They being dependent upon the prosperity of the provinces, we need now a recognition by the federal government of the necessity for conservation of the resources of the provinces. Literally, that matter is strictly a provincial responsibility. But if our resources are depleted and collapse, so will the revenues of the federal government. Some advances have been made but not nearly enough. The economy of British Columbia depends to a great extent on our forest resources. In the past they have been given away or they have been stolen. Our resources have been mined, not forested. In recent years there has been some change in policy, but a provincial government is completely unable to do the kind of reforestation that is required. It is absolutely impossible financially for them to do it. It is to the interest of the federal government to see that reforestation takes place and to see that our forests are not destroyed by fire. As it is in forestry, so is it in almost every other aspect of our national resources. We think it is only reasonable to ask this government, when they consider introducing a bill as they are now doing, to recognize the situation as it exists. If they want to be selfish in their own interests they must play a greater part financially in the conservation or the replacement of the natural resources of all of the provinces of the dominion. They must also play a part in the development of the natural resources. In this modern day and age we are reaching a stage where it is completely impossible for provinces or municipalities to finance required developments. This statement applies particularly in such matters as-and I agree they are within provincial jurisdiction and come under provincial rights-hydroelectric power, the Saskatchewan dam and developments in

the maritimes which they need most desperately but which they are completely unable to provide because of the financial limitations. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is reasonable to ask the government themselves not to take a parochial stand as a national government but to recognize that they have now responsibilities for development and for conservation. As pointed out by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), costs in the fields of highways and education are now completely beyond the fiscal powers of provinces and of municipalities.
I come back to this point. I state quite honestly and bluntly that we as provincial citizens need to have an understanding of our national well-being. I say also that we need to have from this government a national picture or understanding of provincial and municipal well-being. It is most necessary that in this proposal embodied in Bill No. 442 the government recognize that it is not facing up to the problems of Canada as they exist today. I believe that the ten points this group has outlined are important ones. I believe that they are uppermost in the minds of the provincial premiers of the ten provinces of Canada. I should like to consolidate the opinion. I have read the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference. I have read as much as I could of the information supplied. From reading the statements of all the premiers, I think the opinion has been very well put in a telegram from one of the premiers at the request of the editor in chief of the Toronto Daily Star. After being asked his position the premier of Saskatchewan sent this telegram which reads as follows:
. . . new tax proposals as placed before parliament Ottawa almost completely disregard all representations and evidence advanced by provinces supporting our need for more adequate share of direct tax fields jointly occupied by both levels of government. Saskatchewan has consistently argued proposals have three main weaknesses, first level of payments much too low to relieve increasingly serious financial strain on provinces and municipalities with pyramiding costs of education, road building, health and social services, and urban growth. Second, proposals are related solely to revenues from direct tax fields. They make no provision for fiscal needs of poorer provinces struggling to achieve decent minimum services despite scant revenues from alternative tax resources. Third, instead of seeking co-operation of provinces in maintaining efficient co-ordinated tax system new proposals encourage double taxation and may seriously weaken fiscal powers of Ottawa in combatting major economic crisis. Moreover tax proposals advanced in isolation without needed integration in national policies for aiding public investment and economic development, meeting special regional needs, or stabilizing farm income. One redeeming feature of new proposals is that equalization plan for first time clearly recognizes right of all provinces to share more equitably in tax proceeds from personal and corporate income derived from whole country.

From my reading I think that is the consensus of the premiers of the ten provinces of Canada. I want to reiterate this statement, Mr. Speaker. We firmly believe that the interest of Canada demands a new financial understanding between the provinces and the dominion. We believe that, without change in the British North America Act, it demands that the federal government shall give more generous assistance to the provinces and municipalities in meeting responsibilities that were never thought of many years ago. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that in my estimation the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) had a remarkable opportunity at this session and at this time to do a wonderful job for Canada and to do basically what was done at the time of confederation, namely to lay down a plan for the future of this country. I regret that in Bill No. 442 he has not shown any indication that he understands the situation in Canada or the need for revision of fiscal policy so that all governments can meet responsibilities. From all that has been said in the past and what I have read, I think the Minister of Finance should be told of the old Indian proverb that an elephant has two sets of teeth, one for show, the tusks, and one for action inside. I am afraid that this bill, and what has been said in support of it by the government, is for show, for public consumption, but when you get down to the teeth inside, those that mean action, it does not recognize the problems that are facing Canada as a nation.
I sincerely hope-because I see I have only one minute left-that the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, will understand that there is no carping criticism from this group; there is no parochialism. We believe in Canada. We believe in the constitutional rights of the provinces as laid down by the B.N.A. Act. We believe it is possible to produce a plan, a fiscal policy, that will enable all the provinces to come into agreement and thereby not only make it a greater nation but establish more equalized standards in all fields in this dominion. It can be done, and we hope the minister will do something more than is contained in Bill No. 442 at the present time.

I should like to take just a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, to deal with some of the things that were put forward by the speakers who have preceded me. With a good deal of what they have said, I can agree. I find myself in disagreement with some of the things. Certainly, I think we must all agree that the bill that is now before us is one of the most important measures, if not the most important, to come before parliament this year. I hope that it will be treated as an important measure and
6302	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements one that deserves tremendous consideration because from it will devolve the happiness, contentment and welfare of our people for the next five years.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who just finished speaking, in the earlier part of his address mentioned the necessity for greater supervision by the federal government over the economy of Canada. He mentioned the need for thinking nationally and, it seemed to me, as advocating a greater measure of centralization of authority. As I listened to him develop his topic I could not help coming to the conclusion that he apparently forgets one very important matter, that is that all the material wealth that is produced in Canada, all those things we get and enjoy in what we call the standard of living, come from our natural resources. In the last analysis every dollar of taxation taken by all the governments of Canada has to come out of the wealth that is produced by those natural resources. Evidently that is something that my hon. friend forgot. These resources belong to the provinces. The development of these resources was given as a responsibility to the provinces under the British North America Act. The provinces are certainly entitled to the money coming from the development of their resources, first to pay all the costs of development in the provinces, and secondly to take care of the needs of the people in those provinces for services. Now, those are fundamental things,
I think, with which every other province can agree. If the people of any province use the wisdom, vision and care in the development of the resources within its boundaries, then Canada as a whole will be richer and every government in Canada will benefit in some way.
The reverse is true, also. If they do not use wisdom in the development of their resources, if they fail to use care, judgment and efficiency, then everyone in Canada will be poorer. But some benefit must accrue to the people of a province if they do work hard and if they make their resources yield in abundance. If you deny them that benefit of hard work, wisdom and care, then the detriment to development will certainly follow.
While we agree that sharing with the less fortunate provinces in a measure is desirable and is provided for in this bill-it is a principle with which we can all agree-I am sure that if federal supervision of Canada's economy is carried too far or if federal taxation is carried too far, then that great discouragement to the development effort is bound to come and Canada will be poorer and not richer. We have to be careful, therefore, how far we go with these matters. It


seemed to me the hon. member for Vancouver East put forward a principle and then argued against it.
I should like to turn for just a moment to what the hon. member for Eglinton said this morning. I agree with him that the three fields of taxation which are now open on a combined basis between the provinces of the dominion belong just as much to the provinces as they do to the dominion. We could argue from now until doomsday and nobody could possibly prove otherwise. You may bring evidence to support a certain view or you may bring evidence to support just the opposite view. But in balance I am sure the evidence will support the contention that the personal income tax, corporation income tax and succession duties belong just as much to the provincial government as they do to the federal government. Consequently, we cannot look upon the formula the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has worked out as doing anything for the provinces, except in so far as the tax equalization and revenue stabilization do help the poorer provinces. I say that the 10, 9, 50 per cent formula is not completely fair. I think that something more than that could be done. I am not going to suggest a formula that would be more appropriate. The Minister of Finance is capable of doing that because he has all the information.
The second important thing the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) mentioned this morning, and with which I thoroughly agree, was that the provincial governments are not happy about the formula. They do not believe it gives sufficient weight to the needs of the provinces in relation to their responsibility nor to the municipal governments in relation to theirs. The main reason why the provinces are not happy is, as has been stated, the very great problems they face in connection with burdens devolving upon the municipalities. I think the provinces could take care of their own affairs quite nicely if it were not for their creatures the municipalities and the heavy burdens they carry.
The hon. member for Eglinton this morning mentioned the city of Edmonton in my own province, a city that has grown so quickly as to have practically burst at the seams. It has seen an almost unprecedented growth. Over the past several years there has actually been incorporated into that city every month a good size town as far as population is concerned. This means that every one of the services has had to be tremendously expanded and the costs of that expansion have been borne very largely by the people in that city who were already established there. Edmonton, of course, is only one example and there are a great many others

that one could name. Their plight today is a very serious one and it should be given the most earnest consideration by the minister, as I have already indicated in my previous remarks.
There are two main reasons why we are critical of Bill No. 442. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, it proposes to make into law a formula and a set of taxation provisions which the provinces have not approved in conference with the federal government. It is a unilateral proposal placed before the provinces to accept or reject as they wish. If they accept it they go along and take what the federal government is doling out under the 10-9-50 formula. If they reject it, then in order to get revenues they must resort to double taxation which, of course, as the minister knows full well, very few of the provinces would be prepared to do for the simple reason that the people will not put up with double taxation.
The confusion that would result would be monstrous, and that is something we do not want to develop in this country. I look upon this whole proposal as a denial of the partnership principle upon which a smoothly working federal democracy must be based.
I think the time is long past, Mr. Speaker, when any one in Canada with any sense at all could possibly look upon the federal government as the superior and the provincial governments as the inferiors. I think the time has long since passed when we consider that this government has a priority over the provincial governments in the fields of taxation. I think what we have to do is look upon the relationship between the dominion and the provinces as a partnership, and the nearer we can get to a partnership arrangement the better it is going to be.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if the partnership principle is to be observed it must then call for agreements and an approval of a proposal put forward by the Minister of Finance to the premiers or governments of the provinces. If the proposal is not accepted by the majority of the provinces in a good spirit, then it seems to me the best the federal government can do is to say, "All right then, you propose something," and call the provinces together and consider the matter further in the light of the wording of the detailed proposal. When that time comes I am certain that good sense will prevail and that the provinces and the federal government in partnership can work out something that will be acceptable and that will succeed in bringing to the provinces and municipalities what they need in order to be able to carry on.

We stand for partnership, Mr. Speaker, between the provincial and the federal governments and it must be a real partnership. Therefore, the relationship between the dominion and the provinces cannot be satisfactory if there is any thought of their being superior or inferior, senior or junior or a prior claim or this or that in the field of taxation. We have to keep in mind the fundamental need.
We are critical of this measure for another reason, Mr. Speaker. The formula does fall short of providing the provincial governments with a sufficient share of the tax revenues available to the governments of Canada today. The big reason for making that statement, of course, is that the provinces have a terrific problem on their hands in connection with the financing of municipal needs. I am convinced that the major issue in Canada's political life today is the financial inability of the provinces and their creatures the municipalities to perform the duties and carry out the responsibilities allotted to them under the constitution.
I think we have to approach a matter of the kind we are now considering under Bill No. 442 with one question uppermost in our minds, and here it is. Does it do all that is possible to ensure that the provinces and municipalities can fully discharge their responsibilities under the constitutions?
Now, if it does this then we can go forward; if it does not, then we have to oppose it. Does it do all that is possible to ensure that the provinces and their municipalities can fully discharge their responsibilities under the constitution? That is the spirit in which I am trying to consider this measure. The division of powers and responsibilities provided by the British North America Act was, in our judgment, a wise division and I do not think it could have been wiser.
As I consider it, it did at the time divide the powers and responsibilities as wisely as men could possibly have conceived, but over the years since 1867 a great many new situations have arisen which were not foreseen by the fathers of confederation.
A short time ago a study was made in the province of Alberta by some competent people concerning the problem of municipal finances and the relationship between the provinces and the municipal governments. I want to quote just briefly from the report of that study:
When the constitution of Canada was set up by the British North America Act of 1867 even the most forward looking statesmen could hardly have anticipated the complicated functions of government which were to develop over the years.

Almost the total population of Canada was rural. It was an age of individual self sufficiency supplemented by mutual assistance of neighbour to neighbour. The fathers of confederation found this good and saw in this pioneer spirit the future greatness of Canada.
National defence, regulation of international trade, a criminal code, the opening up of the west -these were the concern of government and these could best be handled at federal level. Little was left even for the provincial governments. A member of the legisature for Prince Edward Island sizing up the situation stated "in this house scarcely anything should be left for us to do but legislate dog taxes and the running at large of swine."
The worry was to prevent a government of so little field of responsibility-

-from becoming unduly costly in administration. To quote Galt in his Sherbrook address, "Every effort has been made to reduce the cost of local governments, so that local machinery should be as little costly as possible for it would not do to affront the intelligence of the people and tell them we had devised an expensive kind of machinery to do a very insignificant amount of work."

With such a conception of the role of provincial and municipal governments it is little wonder that the federal government reserved to itself a perfectly free hand in revenue raising by any means of taxation, direct or indirect while it specifically limited the rights of the provincial governments and their creatures, the municipal governments to direct taxation and certain privileges of licensing.
Certain significant trends were soon after to be observed. By 1891 a third of the population was living in urban areas and it was already evident that the local governments must assume new and ever increasing responsibilities little dreamed of by the fathers of confederation. The next half century was to see a continued concentration of urban population with a corresponding decrease in rural population. This trend has continued until in Alberta today there are less than one-third of the people engaged in agricultural pursuits, while in the U.S.A. the rural population is reported to be less than 10 per cent of the total.
I might say that the figures show that the rural population in Canada is something just over 20 per cent. That indicates the trend which has occurred and which places a greater responsibility upon the local government and less, naturally, upon the federal government. We are not overlooking the fact that in time of war or threat of war the federal government must take the prior position; we agree with that. But it seems to us that as peace comes we must recognize the forces which have been at work to change the burden of responsibility largely over to the local governments. That is why I say that the argument that this bill does not sufficiently meet the needs of the municipalities and the provinces is one reason we have to criticize it, and quite severely.

Let me deal for a minute with what the provincial and municipal governments have done to find new ways of raising revenue. I did not realize how resourceful the municipalities have really been over the years until I read this study. It is interesting to note that taxation by municipalities has become a real business. It has developed over the years as a profession to the point where tax commissioners are to be found in municipalities whose sole business it is to hunt up new taxes which may be applied in order to scrounge more revenue out of the pockets of the people. They forget apparently, as do my hon. friends opposite, that every single dollar of taxes must come out of the pockets of the people, and they are the same pockets whether it is the federal, the provincial or the municipal government which does the taxing. Surely they have scraped the bottom of the barrel in many places.
I should like to turn for a minute to indicate what this burden on the municipalities really has been and is now and what efforts have been made to lighten it and what is still left to be done. About six years ago the government of my province approached this matter seriously with a view to determining what could best be done to help the municipalities which were going further and further into debt and finding it more and

more impossible to carry on the services required to be carried on.
That province started to increase direct grants and indirect assistance to the municipalities in an effort to lift their burden. The figures I am giving are taken from the budget address of the Hon. Mr. Gerhart for the year 1955-56 in which he indicated the total amount of assistance which had been granted by the provinces to the municipalities in various forms. I am going to calculate it as a percentage of their total revenues and when I do so I think hon. members will be surprised.
During the six fiscal years ending March 31, 1956 the direct financial assistance granted to the municipalities for the purposes of education, public health, highways, grants in lieu of taxes, municipal assistance, and grants for public aid totalled $208,034,734. There were no strings attached except that the money was marked for the various fields indicated. To give a total amount may not seem to indicate much, but I think it indicates much more when you show it as a percentage of the ordinary revenues of the province for any particular year.
I shall take 1955-56, the last year I have. In that year the total direct grants from the provincial government to the municipal government amounted to $59,069,555 or $60 million in round figures. That is more than 38 per cent of the total revenue on income account of the province. I challenge any province in the Dominion of Canada to match that. They cannot.
Let us go further. In addition to the direct financial grants the government of the province of Alberta gave to the municipalities indirect financial assistance by way of free medical and hospital care for old age pensioners and other public health and welfare services amounting to $7,886,400. That was in the year 1955-56. That brought the total direct and indirect financial grants from the province of Alberta to the municipalities up to $66,955,000, or $67 million in round figures. That may not mean very much unless you show it as a percentage. That sum of $67 million approximately, given in direct and indirect assistance to the municipalities of the province, amounted to 44 plus per cent of the total revenue on income account for that year. That is partnership and I think it stands as an example to Canada.
Of course people will say, "Oh, but you have the money." It is true that our revenues have increased. I can remember my first year as provincial treasurer when I was dealing with a total budget of $20 million,

With those figures before you, you would think the municipalities in my province would be in clover, but the facts were mentioned the other day by my hon. friend from Jasper-Edson (Mr. Yuill), a mayor in a typical municipality, who said that after all this assistance that had been granted by the provincial government to the municipal government, over which he has some jurisdiction, the tax rate on property was 47 mills. Let us stop to think about it. That is a fairly average figure that you would find not only in the municipalities in my province but in every other province. It would be worse in many. I say we have to take those things into consideration when we think about a bill of this kind.
That is one of the reasons I asked the minister, before he brought in this bill for second reading, to get off by himself, take a second look at it, and come back with something that would more nearly meet the need of the provinces and municipalities. I say that a similar picture could be painted in every province in Canada. British Columbia, for example, is looked upon as being a very wealthy province, and will be one without question. As she is now in the throes of a magnificent development, money has to be available for that development. They are trying to build a railway as a Pacific coast outlet for a great part of the country in the north, because the railways would not do it. That is costing them a huge sum of money. They have to build pioneer roads and access roads to ensure the development of their resources.
Education was mentioned the other day. In education what a terrific burden they will

If the minister wants to play the partnership role, he could do no better deed than that. If they are not satisfied; if they feel it is too rigid; if they feel it does not give the minister and themselves flexibility enough to negotiate better arrangements within the framework of the bill, then he should attempt to change it, but I do not believe he should try to put it through and make it law before he has the approval of the provincial governments. So I say there is reason for appreciation of the fact that under the new agreements the provinces are going to get 20 per cent or $115 million more.
My hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit party called that sum niggardly. He called $115 million niggardly. That beats even the famous remark which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is once alleged to have made about $1 million. The only remark I can think of that came close to it was when the former member for Fraser Valley, George Cruickshank, asked the then prime minister, Mackenzie King, after he had announced a $5 million grant to Fraser Valley, and 75 per cent of the cost of flood relief, whether that was just a token payment. I think the comment of the leader of the Social Credit party that 20 per cent or $115 million the first year is niggardly is in that class.
Neither the previous minister of finance nor the present Minister of Finance has ever contended that these agreements are the final solution of an extremely difficult problem. There has been much mention today of the difficulties of governing a federal state. Last year the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and I had the good fortune to have dinner one evening with Prime Minister Menzies of Australia. The talk naturally got around to the subject of federal-state relations. I was amazed to learn that in Australia there is no such agreement or no such bargain. The federal government passes on the budgets of each of the states and decides what money they should be allowed. We have not followed that system. We have tried to negotiate reasonable agreements between the federal and provincial governments.
We Liberals believe in a strong national government. We also believe that in the government of a country of this size it is
