Then as late as 1941 in Halifax at the bar association meeting he was saying this, as reported in the Halifax Herald of April 25, 1941:
"What we need greatly is to look at government from a business point of view," he said, "paralleling methods that a private business with a head office and nine branches would employ to promote more efficiency. Preservation of a nation's integrity must come from a strong centralization feeling," Colonel Drew continued. Canada's main problem was its decentralized government system, and the speaker declared, "solution of that problem would insure continuance of the national structure."
I think those views are worth remembering because, as far as I know, it is the only expression of opinion by anybody in this House of Commons that all power should be concentrated in Ottawa. Most of us believe in the federal system, with a strong national government and effective local governments; and we realize that in our federal system the problem of finance will be very difficult because of the fact that we still have just the one main source of income, namely the Canadian taxpayer.
In this country the problem of the federal government is especially difficult. If we were an old and static society, most public works would be built; but we have one of the most dynamic and most rapidly expanding economies in all the world. So from every part of this country, at every level of government there are demands for more public services; demands to the federal government from provincial governments and to provincial governments from municipal governments. Not only do governments face demands on them, but business in Canada finds tremendous demand on it for added capital, far greater demands than can be met in Canada. So if they want to continue to expand they look abroad for foreign capital. But we cannot satisfy all these demands, either national, provincial, municipal or in business. What we try to do is work out a reasonable compromise, a moderate way which will give top priority to those things of most importance.
The general advantages of these tax agreements have been stressed many times by many hon. members. They include the avoidance of double taxation, something that is extremely important, and the avoidance of unnecessary waste in having duplicate tax administrations. Another point not so often mentioned is the importance of having equal tax rates across all Canada. Before the war, when each province was in the field, the poorer the province the higher were their tax rates so they could get revenues, and therefore the less likely was industry to go to that province because of the higher tax rates.

These tax agreements have helped level that out by providing a uniform system of taxation across the country. More than that, it has given the opportunity to have equalization as between the provinces. Not all our provinces are equally endowed with natural resources; not all our provinces have had equal advantages out of confederation and especially out of our tariff structure. These tax agreements are affording a measure of justice there.
There is one great weakness I have always seen in these tax agreements, the weakness of centralization. I am not thinking of the sort of centralization Colonel Drew was talking about between 1936 and 1941. These tax agreements centralize the tax criticism in Canada on the head of the unfortunate federal Minister of Finance. We do the taxing and get the blame and the provinces get the money and spend it and get the credit. As you know, political kudos more often comes from the spending of public funds than it does from the taxing of these funds of out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers.
Again and again in our history it has been said it is a bad principle that one body taxes and another body spends. In some provinces our school boards are set up in such a way that they fix their requirements and the city council has to raise the money. This has always been a source of friction. One of the things which has a great restraining effect on the government levying taxes is that they must justify to the taxpayers the needs which require that money. When one government taxes and the other government spends, there is not that direct connection or restraint.
We have also heard that the power to tax is the power to destroy. I suppose the destruction envisaged is of business. I tell you that overtaxation by government contains in it the elements of destruction, the destruction of that government. I think every government at every level is very careful not to tax any more than it has to do. But today, of course, the provinces naturally clamour for more money as do the municipalities, and as do certainly the members of the opposition. They would like to raise our tax load and have us merely pass that money over to these agencies to spend. Well, we would be not unlike the cat which pulled the hot chestnuts out of the fire for the monkey.
As I say, I feel the new plan is a great improvement over the old. First of all, as I said, it offers 20 per cent more revenue; second, equalization payments raise the revenues up to the level of the average of the two wealthiest provinces, Ontario and British Columbia. This is a recognition of the uneven tax collections which prevailed when the provinces levied their own taxes. It is

also a recognition that there is a concentration of industry which prospers out of all Canada but which is concentrated in the two central provinces. It is also a recognition of the fact that the provinces in Canada vary greatly in the resources at their command. The very great advantage is, I think, that there is no compulsion. The provinces do not have to sign these tax agreements in order to get the payments to carry out the equalization process, but can levy their own taxes in these fields.
I think, too, there is something to be said for the simplicity of the present formula. It is easily understood; 50 per cent of the succession duties. 20 per cent of the corporation tax that we collect-that is 9 percentage points out of the 45 percentage points making *up the corporation rate-and 10 per cent of the income tax.
The fifth point which is an improvement is that if the provinces do not regard this as sufficient they are quite free to do as Premier Duplessis has done, go out and collect their own taxes. They can still get the equalization payments. Finally there is the stabilization guarantee. This may not be so important now, but it was very important in 1945 as a guarantee that these grants would not fall in the event of a recession or a depression. Our super-optimist here, Right Hon. C. D. Howe, was confident there would be no depression after the war but there were a lot of Cassandras, most of them in the opposition, who foresaw a depression. This guarantee was regarded as very useful then and it is very useful now. Though somewhat in the background it is still an important feature of these agreements.
Let me turn to the criticism now. It is simple enough. We are not paying enough money to the provinces. I can understand the position of the provincial premiers. Theirs is a provincial responsibility, and they want more money to develop their provinces. They do not have the responsibility for federal taxation, so they ask us for more. They certainly have got more in recent years from many sources. This is a striking indication to the people of Canada how frugal has been the federal government in that 10 year period, because our expenditures have gone up only 5 * 5 per cent. It is also a pretty good indication that the provinces and municipalities

Mr. Speaker, the bill submitted to the hon. members of the house for their consideration violates principles which are absolutely indispensable to the survival of this country. It gives a new interpretation, also temporary, to those principles which nevertheless have been clearly set out in the act of 1867. I am no expert in constitutional law, but I do know that all historians and jurists are unanimous in admitting that the constitutional provisions regarding the financial powers of the federal government and the provinces are extremely clear and precise. In the past when the interpretation of some of the provisions had given rise to any ambiguity they had been referred to the courts either by the federal government or by the governments ol the provinces, and even in some cases by private individuals. The courts have handed down their interpretation, which has been duly accepted by jurists and politicians.
On this question of financial relations the federal government has adopted an attitude which to my mind is apt to be highly prejudicial to the future of confederation, whose very basis it is undermining. Since the Rowell-Sirois report there have been a very great number of proposals made by the federal government to the provinces. These proposals have been modified several times because of the criticism to which they have given rise throughout this country. Over this 20-year period all the provinces have in turn expressed their complaints with regard to a policy which leaves their future status highly uncertain. The time at my disposal does not allow me to quote each and every criticism offered on this score by politicians belonging to the main parties of this country, Liberals or Progressive Conservatives, members of the C.C.F. or Social Credit parties.
Each and every proposal submitted since 1937 is contrary to the democratic ideal. They run counter to sound political doctrine, and I am sure that most of the great political figures of the past would be most firm in denouncing them. In a speech which he delivered at Somerset on August 2, 1887, a few days after his appointment as leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfred Laurier stated:
The principle whereby one government collects revenues and another government spends them is altogether false. It can only lead to extravagance.
This principle, denounced by a former leader of the Liberal party, is at the very basis of every financial arrangement entered into by the federal government and the provinces over the last 20 years.
A little later, at a time when Honore Mercier was preparing to call the interprovincial conference of 1887, Sir Wilfrid

These successive Increases in grants, carried out at random and disproportionately, really constitute a means of corruption in the hands of the federal government. All too often this increase in grants paid by the federal government has been little else but the payment of a bill rendered for political betrayal.
The former prime minister of this country and predecessor of the present Prime Minister, Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, speaking in this house in 1930 said:
When on a previous occasion we were discussing this matter of grants from one treasury to another, I said I thought it was an unsound principle; in fact, I think I used the expression that it was a vicious principle to have one body raise the taxes and another body spend the people's moneys thus raised.
Finally the Quebec Liberal newspaper Le Soleil, on February 13, 1947, published an article whose terms still hold true today:
The nine sisters of confederation do not all share the same views on this problem. Six or seven would enjoy receiving financial assistance from the central government and would therefore be willing to renounce for a time claim to those powers of taxation claimed by it. Quebec and Ontario still seem firmly opposed to this plan. Their opposition is based on motives which are sufficiently convincing not to be taken lightly. Any concession is difficult to withdraw later, as has been amply demonstrated by recent experience.
It would be well to remember that the present attitude of the Hon. Maurice Duplessis and Colonel George Drew resembles that formerly adopted by some of their Liberal predecessors. Matters settled by compromise often present both advantages and disadvantages. In the case we are dealing with today, the main cause of the problem is to be found in the federal government's haste to create new provinces whose natural resources are too restricted. They soon found themselves in difficulties either by reason of administrative incompetence or as a result of insufficient revenue. Their situation was further aggravated by the practice of extensive immigration also attributable to the central authorities. There is nothing to justify the statement that such errors will not be repeated. Those conditions make it readily understandable that the defenders of provincial rights should be cautious before being drawn into a project leading to the centralization of powers in the hands of federalists . . .
Such evidence, to which hundreds of other statements could be added, is sufficient to prove that the very principle of these proposals is absolutely false and contrary to the democratic idea. The government collecting the revenue must spend it to fulfil the obligations imposed upon it by the constitution. It is nonsense that a government should collect revenue for the purpose of distributing it to other governments. That is a practice contrary to a principle for which our forebears fought, namely no taxation without representation.

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements
Secondly, to my mind such a policy tends by nature to disrupt the harmony which must exist among all provinces in the Canadian federation. In 1942 a number of provinces felt that they were wronged by the federal proposal. In 1947 other provinces expressed the opinion that they were not treated with justice. This year the same protests are to be heard. This year we even witnessed a meeting of the four Atlantic provinces who wish to join hands for their mutual help and the protection of their interests.
We are witnessing the slow but undeniable formation of a bloc of provinces within confederation. Instead we should have ten provinces closely united and working together for the progress of Canada, with the full co-operation of the federal government. Unfortunately the policy of fiscal agreements will not achieve that unity, because there will always be one or other of the provinces that will feel wronged with regard to its rights, and that is precisely what makes the position of a province like my own extremely difficult in the face of such a problem.
The Quebec government is certainly to be commended for having kept the discussion well above private interests and political expediency. Above all, the position of the Quebec government is a juridical one based upon the soundest constitutional theories. The province of Quebec earnestly wishes to preserve the rights and privileges it was granted by the act of 1867. The province of Quebec is opposed to bargaining, and does not believe that this is a matter to be assessed in dollars and cents. Besides, Canadians of French expression believe this problem affects the rights and privileges they were granted by the act of 1867 and, if we consider the history of financial relations between the federal government and the provinces since 1941, we cannot evade the conclusion that they always endeavoured to safeguard the essential rights of confederation.
Mr. Speaker, you know what the attitude of the Quebec government was in 1937 in the face of the problems set out by the Rowell-Sirois commission, and you know that at the federal-provincial conference of January 14, 1941, the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta were squarely opposed to the implementation of the recommendations of the Sirois report, claiming that that was a peacetime document tending to ruin provincial autonomy. The province of Quebec remained neutral in that discussion and, in April of the same year, the federal government gave up the consideration of the Rowell-Sirois report to ask the provinces, as a provisional arrangement and only for the duration of the war, to vacate the personal
[Mr. Dufresne.l
and corporation income tax fields. In return the federal government offered to indemnify the provincial governments. As a matter of fact, in the period from September 1, 1941, to 1946, the province of Quebec received slightly more than $102 million, or $20 million a year, to allow the federal government to collect the sum of $2,258 million.
In August, 1945, the federal-provincial reconstruction conference was held in Ottawa. In the course of that conference the federal government made to the provinces proposals similar to those contained in the Rowell-Sirois report, but those proposals were a little more generous. In January, 1947, the government at Ottawa submitted a new proposal for grants which was to serve as a basis for the agreements of 1947. Two provinces, Quebec and Ontario, rejected those proposals. Those two provinces reorganized in part their own systems of taxation and levied a new tax of 7 per cent on corporation income. From April 1, 1947, to March 31, 1952, the province of Quebec would have received, had she signed the agreement, a sum of $378,175,000 and during the same period Ontario would have received $444,688,000.
In December, 1950, the provinces met again in Ottawa to discuss the renewal for 1952 of the fiscal agreements of 1947. On the whole the provincial premiers declared themselves in favour of a renewal of the agreements. The premier of Quebec, Hon. Maurice Duples-sis, stated however that, generally speaking, he disapproved the substitution of a system of federal grants for the fiscal powers essential to democratic governments. The premier of Nova Scotia, the late Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, whose government had signed the agreements of 1947, spoke to the same effect:
X do not believe this problem can be met by means of grants. I repeat what I have so often said, namely that the ideal solution would be to divide the responsibilities of the governments and give each of them the necessary sources of revenue to discharge their responsibilities. That is the ideal. I do not know whether we can achieve that end now or later, but it is the end towards which we should strive. Under the circumstances, grants evidently do not appear to me to be the solution.
During the months that followed negotiations continued between the federal government and the provinces, and finally, in 1952, nine provinces decided to sign with the federal government a fiscal agreement for a period of five years. Quebec was the only province that refused to accept the federal grants.
Yet, owing to its fantastic development, the province of Quebec needed additional revenues. In February, 1954, the legislature decided to levy a tax on personal income. That tax amounted to approximately 15 per cent of the federal tax. Such a step was

extremely democratic, because the people of Quebec could accept or reject the government's decision. In fact during the month of June last the electors of the province of Quebec gave a new mandate to the Union Nationale administration and increased its membership in the legislature. I greatly rejoice at the turn of events, which proved to the whole nation that in my province the democratic ideal is still stronger than in any other part of the country. The province of Quebec has not feared to practice the principle of no taxation without representation for which our forefathers fought. It has not feared to base its decisions and actions on that principle.
Today the federal government submits a new series of proposals which would remain in force until 1962. Those proposals are intended to replace the fiscal agreements which will expire next year. In my opinion they are a little less drastic than the previous proposals, and they seem to take into account a little more than in the past the fact that it is a matter of renting provincial rights. They are also more generous because they do not compel the provinces to sign agreements, even of a temporary nature, with the federal government. The signing of a temporary agreement on provincial rights is surely the equivalent of a renunciation, and no government conscious of its responsibilities is happy to abandon its rights and prerogatives.
However, those proposals stem from the same centralizing trend noted in the recommendations contained in the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission. True, the amounts proposed are much more generous than those recommended by the commission which inquired into the fiscal relations between the federal government and the provinces. If we took only that fact into consideration we could say that the provinces acted wisely in compelling the federal government to give them increasingly larger sums over the years. However, the main weakness of that policy is the fact that nobody knows whether those agreements are of a temporary or permanent character. A period of five years is a very short span in the life of a government; in my opinion we must necessarily deal with longer periods.
Those responsible for the federal administration have maintained for almost 20 years that these agreements were temporary, that is, limited to a certain number of years. This may mean that if an emergency arose the federal government could end such agreements, keeping to itself the full tax revenues. That is the interpretation put on those proposals by some public men. Others, on the contrary, feel that these agreements are in fact of a permanent nature even if they are 67509-401

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements modified every five years. They certainly are permanent in peacetime and such, I believe is the true interpretation of all the discussions which have been held on that matter for the last 20 years.
There is no doubt, however, that this system of grants creates uncertainty in provincial quarters, since the provinces do not know whether or not in fact such agreements are permanent or temporary. No one can settle that matter; only the future will tell. Provincial governments carry very heavy responsibilities, especially in this period of economic development and prosperity. Their commitments in the fields of education, welfare, public works and natural resources development are burdensome. They have very heavy responsibilities, as all of them must undertake important projects of a permanent nature for the implementation of which their revenues are inadequate and which must necessarily be paid for through borrowing. I wonder what would happen if a provincial government were to try to borrow from lending institutions a huge sum of money on the guarantee that it would repay such loans out of federal grants. I am almost sure that the financiers would ask how the government intended repaying the loan should an emergency situation arise in Canada. It is the uncertainty of such a policy which, I believe, causes uneasiness among provincial governments.
I am convinced that the most logical and most simple attitude would be to go back to the very words of the act of 1867 and take them as the basis of our policy. It is at least the opinion of the government of the province of Quebec. I take the liberty of recalling that opinion by quoting an excerpt from the brief submitted by the Quebec government to the Rowell-Sirois commission. In fact the stand taken by the province of Quebec is neither complicated nor equivocal. I quote:
In its opinion, confederation is a pact voluntarily accepted and which can be modified only through unanimous consent. The province intends to respect every clause of this pact and expects others to do likewise.
It is at the same time a form of government freely chosen in preference to legislative union, as it can better ensure the protection of the minorities and national development in peace and harmony. That choice was made after careful consideration by statesmen of the two great races and of the two political parties, by statesmen whose unquestionable vision and perspicacity were not obscured by the confusion of a troubled period. The province of Quebec believes that that system is still the best to meet the needs of a large country made up of different races.
In the last analysis, the province of Quebec is willing to co-operate in any endeavour of common interest provided it does not conflict with provincial rights; to help in the implementation of any appropriate and reasonable reform within the framework of the constitution and, generally

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements to work hand in hand with the federal government and other provincial authorities towards the welfare of the nation as a whole, provided the rights of all concerned are respected.
It is a clear and definite stand. The province of Quebec does not wish to take unfair advantage of the difficulties of other provinces. It has always placed that problem above political contingencies and party interest, on the level of principles, through respect for confederation and responsible government.
The other day, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) was deriding provincial autonomy and from the bottom of my heart I pitied him. I pitied him because in the discussion of this matter he could not rise to the true human values. He could not understand that his province had sacrificed grants of millions of dollars out of respect for the rights won by our ancestors. He could not understand that his province could remain faithful to the past, to the memory of those who fought so that we might enjoy freedom. He could not understand that the real political problems are not money problems but questions of principle. He could not understand that in defending these principles his province remained the bulwark of Canadian confederation.
The people of my province, even though they have launched a campaign to attract industries, are a generous people, a people capable of fighting anew for responsible government and in the defence of minority rights. Our forebearers turned down the money and honours of their victors in 1760, but fought 30 years later to preserve the colony for the English crown. The hon. member for Hull should remember history and also keep in mind the sorry record of Adelard Godbout and Georges-Emile Lapalme. They too had forgotten history but they found that the people of Quebec remember the past and want to be faithful to their traditions. The hon. member for Hull should help his party come back to the letter and the spirit of confederation. His constituents would be most grateful to him if he did.

Mr. Speaker, for some time now this house has been engaged in a debate concerning federal-provincial relations. I now propose to deal with this subject from the historic, constitutional and economic points of view.
At the time of confederation Sir John A. Macdonald, father of the Conservative party and its greatest man, was in power. A cursory glance at the report of parliamentary proceedings between February 3 and March 14, 1865, suffices to enlighten us on what this


great leader had in mind at the time. He was careful to state that he would much have preferred a legislative union wherein all powers would have been concentrated in a single central government and that if he gave up that idea it was only because he realized that confederation would have been impossible under such conditions.
While he had to give up his ideal, Sir John nonetheless stated that confederation should take the form of a centralized federal system so that, unlike what had taken place in the United States, or unlike what was to take place later in Australia, residual powers would be left to the federal government, provincial powers, as set out in a moderate list, being essentially those of a local or private nature and adapted to the position of the provinces as Sir John saw it. The federal government would have the power to designate provincial lieutenant governors or to revoke such appointments. Moreover, the federal government was empowered to disallow or set aside legislation passed by provincial legislatures within the year following their adoption.
Even to this day it is not without some surprise that we note the very few difficulties and little discussion to which this distribution of powers between the federal and provincial governments gave rise. Sir John A. Macdonald's explanation was that the delegates had understood the necessity of setting up a strong and powerful central government.
Obviously our political situation has changed a great deal, and for the better, since 1867. To whom do we owe this? First of all to the supreme court and the privy council who, in their interpretation of the constitution, have set things rights by clearly stating the rights of the provinces, by virtue especially of that clause relating to property and civil rights.
It may be of interest at this point to remind the house that in 1867 Hon. Mr. Mer-cier tried to have the constitution amended to the provinces' advantage, but without reference to the federal government. In that year Mercier, who was then provincial premier, called the first interprovincial conference which met in Quebec from October 20 to 28, under the chairmanship of Oliver Mowat, then premier of Ontario. This conference was attended by the premiers and other representatives of five provinces, that is Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Manitoba. Federal representatives had also been invited to attend, but Sir John A. Macdonald declined the invitation on behalf of the government.

The 18th resolution adopted by this conference reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this conference, the various provinces of Canada, through their respective legislatures should, as soon as possible, take such steps as may be required to obtain from the imperial parliament amendments to the British North America Act consonant with the above resolutions.
As was reported by Professor Norman Rogers to the select committee on the British North America Act, a member of which at that time was the present provincial minister of finance for Quebec:
The conference also decided that those resolutions should be transmitted officially to the federal government in order to request its help in bringing about the amendments which were the subject matter of those resolutions. Sir John's federal government refused to support the proposed amendments. However, the resolutions were transmitted through the ordinary channels to the secretary of state for the colonies, who Mr. Rogers said, officially acknowledged receipt of the resolutions but took no steps concerning them.
It would take too long even to summarize all the resolutions but I should like to quote a few brief excerpts.
Thus, it is stated in the preamble that:
[DOT] . . the maintenance of provincial autonomy is necessary to the future well-being of Canada; that, if that autonomy is to be maintained, it is obvious that the constitutional act must be revised and amended.
The following significant words are also to be found:
. . . that several provinces are not in a position to provide, by means of direct taxes or otherwise, for the increase in necessary expenditures and have t!me,t0 time requested from parliament and the federal government an increase in the amount of the annual subsidies.
Oddly enough, nowhere was it deemed advisable to request a new distribution of taxation powers in these long and numerous resolutions from the provinces, in which several amendments to the constitution were sought. Not only that, but it seems that the provinces never considered as a threat to their autonomy an increase in their subsidies. They even went further; and mind you, they were the ones who had provincial autonomy at heart. They passed the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this conference, it is possible to find a basis for the final and unalterable settlement of the amounts payable annually by the dominion to the various provinces for their local purposes and the maintenance of their governments and legislatures.
And the "final and unalterable" amount proposed, should the population exceed at some time one million and a half, was $240,000. Compare the amount proposed with that offered today by the federal government, keeping also in mind the fact that the proposals made today by the federal government 67509-401J

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements are not for a "final and unalterable" amount. They do not involve final agreements, but rather five-year agreements which are moreover subject to review.
Today's problem of federal provincial relations dates back to the financial difficulties experienced by several provinces during the depression years of 1930 to 1935. At that time the western provinces, unable to meet their obligations because of the drought and the fall in the prices of agricultural products, were on the brink of bankruptcy; and all across Canada unemployment placed an intolerable burden upon local governments. The federal government had to give temporary financial assistance to Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It had also to take over the task of solving the unemployment situation as best it could. The Rowell-Sirois commission was appointed in 1937 to study this urgent problem and, without going into details, it may be said that the present agreements are the results of the commission's recommendations.
The commission had, in effect, recommended (a) exclusive federal jurisdiction in the field of personal income tax, of corporation income and of succession duties; (b) full federal responsibility for unemployment; (c) acceptance by the dominion of charges entailed by provincial debts; and (d) payment of subsidies by the federal government so as to put all provinces in the position of providing average provincial services without having to increase the incidence of taxation.
The federal government has since then accomplished more than was recommended in the report, and has done all in its power to come to an agreement unanimously acceptable to the federal government and to the provinces. Far from assuming a rigid and arbitrary approach, as was claimed by some for political purposes, it has on several occasions compromised with the provinces and accepted their suggestions.
I leave now the historic aspect of the question to deal as briefly as possible with its constitutional aspect and, finally, with its economic aspect. Let us see what the constitution has to say in the matter. I shall just read out

3. The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.

What do these paragraphs mean? They mean exactly what they say. First of all, the federal government has the exclusive right to tax, by any method or system it chooses, either direct or indirect, and that only for their own provincial purposes may the provinces resort to direct taxation.
Indeed, were the federal government to exceed its powers, either in levying income tax or succession duties, what would happen can easily be imagined. Thirty-five years ago, that is in 1917, the Conservative party introduced the federal income tax. Is it possible that during this long period, from 1917 to 1952, no provincial government, no individual taxpayer would have raised the so-called unconstitutionality of this act in order to have it declared ultra vires and unconstitutional? Everybody knows that such an argument is absolutely groundless. I need not stress the point any further. There is obviously nothing in this to prejudice provincial autonomy, no more now than in 1917, when the law was first introduced by the Conservative minister of the day, Sir Thomas White.
Whatever may be said today, nobody could convince us that the tax rental agreements between the federal government and the provinces are contrary to the spirit of the constitution, or an encroachment upon provincial autonomy. Is this not the very same sort of agreement that Ottawa concluded with all signatory provinces? Are these agreements not clear and definite? They are in black and white, and anybody who can read should be able to realize it. Are they not strictly and absolutely fair? In other words, is not the federal government guaranteeing each province an amount which not only is equal to the amount of taxes the provinces are losing, but is even more substantial?
The federal government is in no way encroaching upon this provincial field, because under the very terms of those agreements royalties and rights concerning their natural resources are levied and collected by the provinces themselves who also collect income tax on mining or forestry operations. Anyone doubting it has only to read, inter alia, section 3 of the agreement between Canada and British Columbia signed on July TO, 1952. All agreements signed to date have in effect been signed for a period of five years. The fact is that several provinces

to veterans, family allowances, etc., that whole program which the federal government undertook to implement and which it has actually implemented under agreements with all of the provinces. Let us add about $440 million interest on a national debt incurred almost entirely during the two great wars. Finally let us add $300 million paid annually to provincial governments in grants or under tax rental agreements. That leaves only $700 million for all other services combined.
Now let us consider whence these revenues are derived to meet these extraordinary expenditures; what sources of taxation produce these revenues. A government, to remain in power, must levy fair, equitable and well balanced taxes. Income tax is the main pillar of the whole structure; it brings the federal government more than $2i billion, divided just about evenly between personal and corporation income taxes. The amount levied through income tax therefore corresponds to our defence expenditures and part of our social security expenditures. Another $1 billion of national revenue is derived from what I would call domestic taxation on commodities, that is the 10 per cent sales tax paid by manufacturers to which, in several cases, is added a special 15 per cent excise tax, and the very high taxes on alcoholic beverages, beer, wine and cigarettes. Over and above all these we have customs duties which yield from $300 to $400 million, and succession duties which, although they yield no more than $30 to $40 million, are most useful in certain cases as a means of controlling income tax.
I have said enough to start drawing conclusions, the main one being that the federal government cannot give up direct taxation, and income tax in particular, without giving up its whole national defence and social security program. It is inconceivable that the provinces should take over national defence; not only would this be ultra vires, but it would cause chaos and anarchy. Neither is it conceivable that the dominion should give up nor that the provinces should take over the entire responsibility for social security, a responsibility which the federal government assumed at their request; a responsibility which, as I said, cost $1 billion and which would double every provincial budget. Except for Quebec and Ontario, such an arrangement would in no time bring ruin and bankruptcy to all the provinces, even if the income tax were returned to them.
What, then, is the solution? For the moment there can be no other than the status quo, with the compensation provided for under temporary tax rental agreements.

Do the tax rental agreements really infringe upon provincial autonomy? Ever since confederation grants have been paid under the constitution. At first these grants were proportionately higher than they are today, accounting for more than half the provincial revenues. But no one ever complained, nobody ever asked that they be withdrawn; on the contrary, every one of the provinces without exception constantly endeavoured to have them increased. They are hardly justified today in saying, "Stop handing out federal grants and let us levy more taxes". So we may safely say that federal grants do not infringe upon provincial autonomy.
Federal tax rental agreements are voluntary and temporary. No province is under any obligation to sign an agreement, and when it does so it is only for a fixed period of time. Proof that the agreements are beneficial to the provinces may be found in the fact that several of them, when the agreements expired, felt the need to renew them and actually did so. Far from encroaching upon the provincial field, the agreements guarantee and safeguard provincial autonomy.
The fact that the federal parliament levies income tax does not deprive the provinces of their right to do so. But it is easily seen where this would lead. What would happen if 11 governments resorted to the same taxation? Is it not more reasonable, fair and economical to have but one collecting body, which then passes on to the provinces their rightful share on a per capita basis?
From the point of view of distributive justice, Canada's wealth being mainly centred in Ontario and Quebec where the more important corporations have their headquarters, and considering the fact that the other provinces contribute their share to the development of such corporations, that our-first allegiance is to Canada and the fact that the prosperity or poverty of one part affects: the country as a whole, is it not fair and just to have our income tax centralized and them distributed, as I said, on a per capita basis?.'
I sincerely believe that the federal-provincial tax agreements can but strengthen our federal system. Such agreements guarantee each provincial government a sound financial basis and full freedom of action, as well as complete autonomy in relation to all matters which, by virtue of our constitution, come within its jurisdiction.

What I have in mind, Mr. Speaker, is that I think we have lost sight of the point that the federal government in its taxation policy has taken to itself a large portion of taxes, and has not returned sufficient of the moneys collected to the provinces for the particular items the minister has cited as being constitutionally the responsibility of the provinces. One way in which that matter could be settled very easily would be to turn the money back to the provinces and let them deal with it.
3 agree in principle that there should be some legislation which would provide fiscal arrangements to equalize payments as between those provinces which have a great deal of natural resources and those provinces which have fewer natural resources. I think that is right in principle and, as a matter of fact, as I recall it the premier of the province of British Columbia reiterated that statement in his presentation to the government on December 14, 1952.
I think it is unfair to deplore the fact that the provinces are making demands on the federal government. The only reason for the provinces making demands on the federal government is because the federal government has already taken the money from the provinces, and they want back more money than they are presently receiving. To put forth the argument that there are provinces asking for help and therefore we

have to go out and increase taxation is simply putting the cart before the horse. What we have to face up to is that the federal government collects the money and it is the duty of the provinces, as it were, to try to get back their fair share.
I go along with those who say that we should avoid as much as possible duplication of taxation. I think that is only common sense; but I must say again that I do not agree with the idea that when the federal government collect money they alone have the sovereign right to spend that money. I agree that there have been compensatory payments to the provincial governments, but those governments feel that those payments have not been enough. I think the minister pointed out in his statement that this is true. He said that the federal government have found themselves paying out money and instituting things which are constitutionally the responsibility of the provinces. That being the case then the federal government, rightly or wrongly-I am not arguing the point-have certainly found themselves in the position of holding the purse strings while the provinces find themselves in the position that they must come to ask for assistance because the money has been taken from them.
Some reference was made by the minister to the responsibility of the federal government as a unifying force. Referring to the federal and provincial governments the minister said, as reported at page 5987 of Hansard of July 16:
Each has its own assigned responsibilities, but it is the federal government that must provide the unifying force that makes a nation out of what would otherwise be a confederacy of the loosest sort.
The question which arises in my mind is how good a job has this government been doing, when we find across Canada echoes of discontent in the matter of provincial-federal relations. If this government is going to provide that unifying force there must certainly be ultimate co-operation on the part of the federal authority. Every means must be taken to get the provinces to come and work out something which will be mutually satisfactory to all concerned. I do not for a moment consider that Bill No. 442 is going to help in creating that unifying force in Canada. The reason I say that is that Bill No. 442 seems to be a mould into which this government expects the provincial governments to fit. If that sort of thing is considered by this government to be a unifying force, then I cannot agree with it.
Where is the financial policy of this government going to lead us in the field of social services? As I said before, I am not arguing

the point as to whether the federal government should or should not be in that field. The thing that is important is the fact that the federal government's financial policy has led to a 47 per cent loss in the purchasing power of recipients of social assistance, and this is also true of pensioners and those who invested money years ago in annuities. It is my opinion that the present thinking in Canada is that it is the responsibility of the federal government to bring those who have been thus adversely affected by federal financial policy to a position where they will have the same purchasing power they had ten years ago. That would mean that all recipients of social assistance, all pensioners and those living on annuities would have their particular funds brought up by 47 per cent.
Of course the first thing we will hear echoing across the country is that that would be inflation. I do not agree that that is necessarily so. In the first place, such an increase of purchasing power could be distributed to those people by the creation of money by the Bank of Canada, just as the ordinary banks create money needed for lending to industry or for other purposes. If this money were created by the Bank of Canada for the government it should be spent into circulation by increased payments to recipients of social assistance and those who are on pensions and annuities.
The money so created and issued to the government and sent into circulation in that manner would find its way as cash payments to the retailer, which would be reflected into the business of the wholesaler and the manufacturer. In many cases the manufacturer would then be able to pay off a certain percentage of his bank loan and having done so, the money would go out of existence at that point. Any time a person pays off a bank loan that amount of money goes out of existence and reduces the over-all money supply of the nation by that amount, just as borrowing money from the bank increases the money supply.
I submit that there is no reasonable ground to believe that this is going to cause inflation. What it does mean is that these people who to my mind are the responsibility of the national government in this respect, because it is the national government that has control of monetary and financial policies in this country, would have their purchasing power brought up to where it was ten years ago. If the financial policies of this government have robbed our people of 47 per cent of their purchasing power it should be the duty of the government to bring back the purchasing power of those people to where it

Let us take a quick look at what has happened to our taxing picture over the last several years. In 1930 the federal taxing authority took 40 * 5 per cent of our tax dollar. In 1951 they took 70-9 per cent. That is an increase of 30-4 per cent of each tax dollar. The provincial take in 1951 was 17-2 per cent compared with 20-2 per cent in 1930, and the municipalities received 11-9 per cent in 1951 compared with 39-3 per cent in 1930.
Let us face facts. The municipalities are receiving less than one-third of the portion of the tax dollar that they received in 1930, but their obligations have increased tremendously in proportion. In fact it was this government which instituted the Rowell-Sirois commission from which the ideas which are now prevalent in our federal system had their main source.
I do not think we should accept statements of a vintage which preceded the report of that commission as expressing the present views of the people who made them at that time. There are many more current observations on this problem which is before the house. I should like to bring the house up to date at least to post-war comments on what has been happening in our federal system.
The earliest and most extensive conference after the war, when an effort was made to sort out the problems which had arisen as a result of the centralization of the war, was the conference of 1945-46. That was quite an extensive and extended conference, at which there was ample opportunity for the statesmen of this country to express their views on the fiscal relationship between the provinces and the central government and to try to point the direction which should be taken in the years that lay ahead.
It was clear that the country was moving out of a wartime era into one of peace. The conference was named by Mr. King a conference on reconstruction, and it was a conference on reconstruction. Its purpose was to try to chart a course by which some of the effects of the concentration of authority in Ottawa during the war could be sorted out effectively and to the satisfaction of the different governments of Canada.
I should like to remind the house of the view that was expressed on that occasion by one of the maritime premiers, namely Hon. Mr. MacMillan who represented the province of Nova Scotia. On August 7, 1945, as found at page 127 of the report of that conference, he read a report which was presented to the federal authorities as expressing the view of the province of Nova Scotia. It was a report compiled by Dr. Dawson, and was in these terms:
The province along with all other provinces had been manoeuvred by war exigencies into a position where it will be extremely difficult to resist future dominion demands for extensions of power. The relinguishment of a large part of the provincial taxing power through the dominion-provincial agreements of 1942 and constitutionally valid but temporary wartime powers assumed by the dominion have given the federal government a whip hand which it apparently does not intend to give up readily. It is, however, the dominion's power to levy unlimited taxes in all fields that is the big club that can be held over provincial heads. If, for example, the dominion should persist in 
imposing an initial 30 per cent income tax, should increase its existing rate of succession duties and should retain a heavy corporation tax, it could render almost completely nugatory the provincial power to impose those direct taxes which are essential to solvency. For any provincial tax imposed in addition to these onerous dominion levies would impose an intolerable burden on the taxpayers of the province. The province in short has lost its bargaining power. It might, it is true, have lost it without the war, but in ordinary times no dominion government would have had the temerity to dictate the proposals contained in the agreement of 1942 without giving more in return and without a long period of negotiation and bargaining.
That is a fairly forthright statement by one of the Atlantic provinces presented in 1945, when the pattern was being set.

When we rose, Mr. Speaker, I was speaking about the federal government's expenditures in the field of provincial jurisdiction. A figure of $900 million was mentioned as the sum total of a variety of social welfare expenditures which are said to come in this category.
I think it is well to place beside this statement the figures for tax collections by the federal government in the three fields of direct taxation, that is the personal income tax, corporation income tax and succession duties. Those are the three fields of taxation which the federal government has enjoyed almost exclusively and which have become a great source of the additional revenues which are now focused in Ottawa, as contrasted with the period before the war when there was little money raised in these tax fields.
I have the figures for 1954. They are not the latest, but will illustrate the amounts which these three taxes bring into the federal coffers. In 1954 the personal income tax brought in $1,284 million. The corporation income tax was very little short of that; it was over $1 billion. The succession duties, the third of these direct taxes, brought in over $73 million; at least that was the federal tax, I think, before the allowance for the provinces that have concurrent taxes in the estate duties field. The total of these three taxes was $2,418 million or about five times the total revenues and expenditures of the federal government in 1939. It is at least over four times the total amount that was received in Ottawa and spent by the federal government in that year. This $2-4 billion from these three fields of taxation shows the expansive power of these taxes in a growing economy. It is these taxes which are the subject of this bill.

If you add up the amount of money which is being paid to the provinces under the tax rental agreements, which is a total of $350 million for the current year, and the amount which is being paid out by the federal government and for which it is taking great credit in those fields of provincial jurisdiction, some $900 million, you arrive at $1,200 million, which is still only 50 per cent of the amount of money the federal government is receiving from these taxes which, as I say, are properly, on any legal basis of construction of the constitution, the joint preserves of the provincial and federal governments. That is the result, even crediting the dominion with

The items making up the $900 million are well known. They are family allowances, $383 million; old age assistance, $91-4 million; blind persons pensions and allowances, $3 million; general health grants, $33-7 million; other grants, $29 million, making a total of $540 [DOT] 7 million. Then on top of that you have the old age security payments which are not shown on the balance sheet because they are supposed to be financed out of separate taxation. This will amount to $367 million in the current fiscal year, making a total of $908 million.
I think in order to maintain any sense of proportion in considering the position of the provinces, one has to set off those figures of tax collection against the claims of the federal government that by this $900 million they are lightening the load of the province. Looking at the problem from that point of view, if the provinces are content to credit the federal government with $900 million paid on their account; if they feel that is the best way that tax money could be expended in the meeting of their responsibilities, then all right. But that is not the proposition with which we are confronted. The provinces have had these payments made by the federal government and have, it is true, received advantage from them, but these have not been made under any comprehensive scheme of adjustment of responsibilities and of revenues.
The minister himself has laid down as one of the three principles by which he is activated in trying to arrive at a fair disposition of this matter, the proposition that the provincial revenues should be commensurate with their responsibilities. There are two sides to the equation. There are responsibilities and there are revenues. It is a question of whether the provinces would prefer to have these revenues or to have the dominion government collect and spend them in the interests of the provinces in the discharge of their duties.
I recall that the other day I said that one of the provincial premiers of the same political persuasion as the Minister of Finance, Mr. Hicks, in dealing with this problem in a speech in Toronto before the Canadian Club, said that these fields of provincial responsibility, which are being dealt with in a way by these large payments made from the federal treasury, have been transferred to


Ottawa unwittingly and without the decision of the governments concerned or the decision' of the people, and this did not seem to be a fair way of modifying our federal constitution.
Those figures might be supplemented, I think, with some other reflections on the sources of federal revenues. I have a table here which shows the amount of money collected in the year 1955 from each of these three direct taxes from the various provinces of Canada, and as I am speaking to this matter largely as the representative of an Ontario constituency, I think it is proper to put on the record the amount of tax that comes from that province in these three fields.
In 1955 the individual income tax paid by people in Ontario was $633 million out of a total collection of $1,284 million, roughly 50 per cent of the total income tax collection in the whole of Canada. The same thing is true in the corporation profit tax field. The collection from corporations was $512 million from the province of Ontario out of a total of $1,060 million, again just short of half. In the succession duty tax field the collection in Ontario was $34,366,000 out of a total of $73,944,000.
I do not propose to pursue that except to show, as I will presently, that the federal government is enjoying great revenues because of the industrial expansion and activity which this country has experienced in the post-war years, and that generated by those activities there is a corresponding need on the part of the provinces to provide the services.
If all these direct taxes collected in Ontario were added together they would be in excess of $1,100 million and if one placed against that total the amount of the federal payment to Ontario under the 1952 tax agreements one would find it is a small and pitiable amount in comparison. The minister will know the amount, but I think the current year's payment to Ontario is in the neighbourhood of $163 million. That is about 14 per cent of the yield of those three taxes in that one province.
There is one other set of figures which I ask the house to permit me to give, though figures are not usually very interesting, and that is a comparison of the federal grants, or payments as I prefer to call them, under the tax agreement to the province of Ontario, with the payments the province has had to make to its municipalities to maintain their solvency without excessive taxation of the citizens of those municipalities.
I will give you first the federal payment to Ontario under the 1952 agreement. They

begin in the fiscal year 1952-53 at a sum of $123 million. For the current year 1956-57 there is shown a payment of $151 million. I believe I said it was $163 million but actually $151,700,000 is the estimated payment to Ontario this year. That is an increase of 23 per cent over the period of five years which the agreement covers. I tried to give figures on this when I spoke on the resolution, but X have them documented a little more carefully now. The grants of all kinds which the province of Ontario made to its municipalities in 1952-53 represented a total of $97,665,000. I call the attention of one of the hon. members from the province of Alberta to this figure, because he challenged any other province to match the grants which the province of Alberta has been making to its municipalities. In 1952-53 the sum of $97,665,000 was paid by the province of Ontario to the municipalities.
I would like to recall to the house that that is very largely the result of the foresight of the present Leader of the Opposition, who instituted grants of that kind for educational purposes in 1943. The necessity for them has been substantiated throughout the years, and these educational grants comprise a very large part of these payments from the provincial treasury to the municipalities of Ontario.
In the course of the five-year period the $97,665,000 rose to $184,700,000 for this current year, 1956-57. That is almost double- in fact it is 97 per cent more-as compared to the 23 per cent increase in the same period which the province received under its arrangements with the federal government.
I was referring, Mr. Speaker, to some quotations which are more recent than those which the Minister of Fisheries was able to find. Apparently he has not received any books in his library since 1939 or 1940, but there are the proceedings of the conference held in 1945-46 at which a good deal was said about this principle of grants as a solution to the relationship between the central government and the provincial governments. I presented Mr. MacMillan's statements on the subject, and I would like now to refer to a statement or two made by the present Leader of the Opposition who attended that conference as the premier of Ontario. Mr. Drew at page 14 of the proceedings of April 29, 1946, said this:
There is no question of generosity on the part of the dominion government or lack of generosity. There is no question of selfishness on the part of the provinces or of lack of selfishness. What we are discussing here is the allocation of taxes paid by the same taxpayers across Canada. What we are seeking is a procedure by which these combined taxes may be channelled into the most effective courses to the advantage of all the people who live in the nine provinces.

That is still the problem today. It is not a question of centralization or not; it is a question of allocation for the benefit of the people of Canada in their two capacities as taxpayers and recipients of the services of the federal and provincial governments.
At page 21 Mr. Drew said:
The whole system of subsidies is wrong and should be brought to an end just as soon as a complete and exhaustive analysis of our tax structure can be carried out for the purpose of establishing a new tax structure in Canada.
He went on to quote a learned authority on public finance, Professor Jensen, who said:
Subsidies here defined as transfers from the central to the intermediate or local governments merely as devices for balancing intermediate and local budgets in normal times should not be tolerated and as devices for aiding the latter in emergencies they should be scrutinized with the utmost care. They tend to weaken the responsibility of the receiving governments by making them clamorous beggars at the door of the federal government.
Then follows quotations which have been heard in this house at least once, from Sir Wilfrid Laurier, on the same subject. Mr. Drew at page 22 said:
All Canadians must face the very dangerous theory inherent in all this and now affecting huge sums of taxpayers' money, namely, that one government in Ottawa should collect money without any definite limit and hand it over to governments which can spend it without the responsibility of collecting it, without answering directly to the taxpayers who provide it.
In case some hon. members may say this is an indication that the Leader of the Opposition or this party is against subsidies in any form, I will say now we do not take that position. We recognize the principle of the equalization grants which have appeared under various names such as fiscal need grants and national adjustment grants, as they were called in the proposal which the Ontario government made in 1945. The Leader of the Opposition made it clear that he recognized that this was an essential factor of our federal system, due to geographical and other conditions of inequality, when he said:
Before closing these remarks it perhaps should be said again in this open conference that the Ontario government has at all times expressed its belief in the principle of fiscal aid to those provinces which from time to time require special financial assistance and that Ontario which proposed the setting up of a national adjustment fund for that purpose keeps that proposal before this conference.
That position was made abundantly clear when the Leader of the Opposition spoke here a week ago Monday during the resolution stage.
I should like now to refer to the background of Ontario's need for revenue of its

In recent years it has been increasing at an annual rate of nearly 150,000. This growth of nearly 3 per cent annually, which is nearly double the annual rate of increase in the United States and exceeds that of the rest of Canada, stems, of course, from two main forces-our natural increase and immigration. That created the responsibilities which have been mentioned here and which devolved upon the municipalities. The birth rate which has increased substantially has apparently reached a plateau and is continuing at that high level. The normal family although it is not what it used to be in the days of my youth, seven, eight or nine children, but is now three, four or five children, is larger than it was immediately before world war II.
On this basis Ontario in the next five years will have 700,000 more people, and it is expected that the population of the province will be 6 million by 1961 and 8-2 million by 1975. That is really a remarkable figure when one realizes that no one would have dared to predict a population of 5 million for Ontario by 1965 just a few short years ago. All this of course brings responsibilities. The rise in number of births means that there is a larger proportion of younger people in the population. Today there are one million people in the elementary schools of Ontario, and it is estimated that in 10 years three-quarters of a million more will have to be


provided for. That is an increase equal to three-quarters as many as there are now, in the short space of 10 years.
Then there is the problem created by the need for skilled and technical workers in all fields. The serious shortage of engineers and technicians has received considerable attention, but there is also a shortage of physicians, physicists, chemists, accountants and virtually all professional classes, even economics. There is a desperate shortage of dentists. This is a condition for which there appears to be no immediate remedy. I think the people of this province and of this country must be prepared for a shortage of highly skilled workers during the next quarter of a century.
I see my time is running out, but I should like to say a word about capital investment in the province. In the last 16 years nearly $19 billion has been invested in the province of Ontario, and very little of that was due to the efforts of the government in Ottawa. There are only two items in the list of factories, machinery and equipment, commercial buildings, housing, utilities, schools, highways, roads, hospitals, waterworks, sewage and similar undertakings to which the federal government has made any contribution. I refer to housing, where loans have been made, and to highways, where there has been some contribution to the trans-Canada highway. In the case of hospitals there have been some grants in aid made jointly with the province.
I have here the figures of the expenditures in some of these major fields such as education, the provision of highways, the provision of sewage systems and other services for the industrial parts of the country during the next 10 years. These will run to a total of something like $8 billion. That is a lot of money for a province which has no great tax field, which has only a certain amount of leeway, which is living in a sense within the confines of a strait-jacket or in a suit which is too small for its present size. That is a problem which this house has to deal with in considering what kind of agreement should be made between the federal government and the provinces, none of which are satisfied at this stage.

Mr. Speaker,
I believe it will be a matter of general regret in this house and perhaps elsewhere that this bill is brought before the house when we are coming close to the end of the session. The great importance of this matter has been emphasized by various hon. members. We are now discussing the question of dominion-provincial relations generally and tax agreements in particular, which have to do with the whole national economy and the

survival of the nation as a whole. Had the bill been brought in earlier and submitted to a standing committee after second reading it is quite possible that we might have had the advantage of the experience and knowledge of experts in the field of dominion-provincial relations, who could have offered some sound advice. However, now that we are faced with the question I should like to draw attention to one or two principles which have not been emphasized too strongly up to this point.
Before doing so I should like to refer to something said this afternoon by the Minister of Fisheries when he made his contribution to this debate. The main theme of his contribution seemed to be the claim that this measure should be considered as satisfactory because it was rather generous, because it represented an increase of approximately $115 million over the previous arrangement on the part of the federal treasury, or about a 20 per cent increase. It was on that theme that the minister built up his argument.
Those of us who regard this problem as serious, as a nation-wide problem and certainly not one that should be used as a political hot potato to be chased around, rather deplore that sort of approach by one of the ministers of the government. Had it come from one of the private members supporting the government one could put it down as a member arguing the case for the party he supports; but coming from a cabinet minister, placing it on the level that the government is being very generous and that the opposition members really have nothing to complain about because what is being offered now represents $115 million more than what was offered under previous arrangements, is putting it on a very narrow basis.
In my view the real question is not whether this offer represents a larger amount, either in dollars or in percentages, as compared with what was offered in previous years. The real question is whether this bill is going to be effective in bringing about a solution of the problem that has been before this parliament and this nation for over 25 years, the problem of finding a means of sharing the available revenues in the most equitable, efficient and sensible manner among various levels of government. It is not a question of whether this represents an increase of $115 million or 20 per cent; it is a question of whether the revenues that are available, whatever the figure may be, can be so arranged as between the provincial governments and the federal government- and, of course, including the municipalities- so that the people of Canada, who are after all citizens of the same nation whether they
