Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements live in one province or another, will feel that their tax dollar is being as efficiently and sensibly used as possible in the various fields.
I think we would be further ahead if we approached it from the point of view of each one placing himself in the position of the taxpayer of this country, not as a Manitoban or an Albertan or a Torontonian but as a citizen of Canada, and asking ourselves this question: "When I part with my tax dollar, how do I want it spent, and how do I think is the most efficient and productive way in which that money can be spent?" If we can answer that question to the satisfaction of the taxpayer of this country, regardless of whether he lives in one part of the country or another, I am sure he will feel that we are approaching this matter from a national point of view.
Of course the Minister of Fisheries, in making his speech, used part of it to welcome a newcomer to his party. I could not pass that up, because it was a rather unusual situation that I have not previously witnessed in this house, as a good many have not. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre made his speech this afternoon, which certainly cannot be characterized as a maiden speech-he made that some time ago-but, considering that we were witnessing the first speech of a new Liberal, we shall have to call it a maternity speech. I hope he is successful in convincing his constituents-
Don't worry about him. Start worrying about yourself.

-that the party on the basis of opposition to which he was elected three times has suddenly changed so much that he has been put into the position of having to defend that party and the government. However, I leave that to him.
The problem that is before the country today, and has been before it for about 25 years, is the inadequacy of tax bases for the provinces upon which to raise the necessary revenue to fulfil their responsibilities under our constitution. Secondly, it is the problem of the inequality of standards of living and standards of services offered in the various provinces across Canada and the desire of the Canadian people to set up some sort of minimum standard, at least, which should be enjoyed by every Canadian in order that he may have a feeling of national pride that as a Canadian he has certain inalienable minimum rights and privileges. Third, it is the problem of the inefficiency and inconvenience of what is called double taxation.
I do not like to use the term "double taxation", because I think it leaves the wrong
6332	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements impression. When people hear the term "double taxation" the inference is created that because the federal parliament imposes certain taxes and the provincial legislatures impose certain taxes, that means the taxes are going to be twice as much or that necessarily they will be higher than if they were left to one jurisdiction alone. Of course that is not so. The term "double taxation" really means that you have taxes imposed by two different jurisdictions upon the same taxpayer, perhaps using two different methods and standards of collection. I think it is the desire of Canadian people generally that there should be a minimum of duplication in the raising of revenues, not because of the taxation involved but because it is an inefficient and inconvenient way in which to raise the necessary revenues.
Those seem to be the three central problems. I think we have to go behind them and ask ourselves also, how did those problems arise? Quite evidently this is something that has not arisen during the past few years but has been a sort of accumulation over a long period of years. How did we get into that condition? First of all the British North America Act, which is accepted as Canada's constitution, is now 89 years old. When the fathers of confederation met and conceived this nation and made the request to the parliament of Great Britain for an enactment to set up confederation, no one at that time could have conceived some of the developments that have taken place.
I should like to draw attention to one or two of those developments that I do not believe have been mentioned up to now. One is the mass concentration not only of wealth but of financial power in certain parts of this country. When Canada became a nation there was a sort of equality. Perhaps it was an equality of relatively low standards of living at that time, but at least there was a sort of equality within the various components of this nation. We had not felt the effects then of the tariff structure, because that had not yet come into play. We had not yet started feeling the effects of the building up of huge corporations which has had the effect of concentrating wealth and power in certain areas of the country. But as time went on we began to feel those effects, and in my view we are now in a position where I think in the next two years, probably, or in the next five or ten years, we are going to feel those effects at an accelerated rate. It is my view that the concentration of financial power is increasing at a greater rate today than it was 10 years ago, and cerainly at a much greater rate than 20 years ago. As we go into the field of
[Mi. Zaplitny.]

specialization, automation and the high speed business methods of the new era, we are going to find that the concentration of financial power is going to accelerate and the problem is going to become greater and greater and more acute in a short time.
Then, of course, there have been the effects of the two world wars. It is not necessary for me to review what those effects were; they are well known to the members of this house and to the people of this nation. We know that under the stress of the first and second world wars certain things were done which had the effect of disrupting the normal occupations and methods in this country, and had the effect of further accelerating this accumulation of financial power.
I should like to mention here that apart altogether from the kind of legislation we are now considering, and the dominion-provincial conferences which we have once in a while, there are some things that are basic to this problem of the concentration of financial power, which will have to be faced.
I believe there are two things that can prevent that concentration from becoming far more serious than it is. One of those has been advocated by this group on many occasions; finding fields of public ownership, particularly of public utilities, in which the public themselves can participate in the management of their own affairs and therefore, of course, in the management of their own revenues. We can tax as we like, but we must recognize what has been pointed out by many economists, not the least of whom, if I may call him such, is the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), who in many of his speeches when he was premier of Manitoba made this kind of argument which I think was very sound. I doubt if he would make it now, but I believe it is quite sound.
He pointed out that the whole business of taxation, particularly the taxation of corporations, is in one sense an illusion because, as he pointed out in one of his speeches at that time, all the corporations do is pass on the taxes imposed upon them in the form of increased prices of the products they sell to the public, so that in the end the consumer pays every nickel of taxation in this country. You may say that we impose so much individual income tax, so much sales tax, so much corporation tax, so much of other kinds of taxes, but in the end it is the individual consumer who buys and pays for the products that are manufactured or produced in Canada, who pays every nickel of the taxation, because, it is all passed on to him in the prices of the goods he has to buy.

That being so, the only real way in which the people of Canada through their various levels of government can have full and complete control over their own revenues is by participating in the greatest possible way in the management of their own affairs. One of the ways in which that can be done is through public ownership, whether it is done on the federal level, the provincial level or the municipal level. The other way it can be done in order to avoid this concentration of financial power in the hands of a few corporations in certain areas of the country is through co-operative ownership. In my opinion this is one of the finest ways in which the production of wealth and the revenue derived from that wealth can be kept within the community to serve the needs of that community rather than having it all drained off and channelled into one huge financial empire, with no loyalty to any part of the country, and which only cares about its own affairs.
I believe these two factors have to be taken into account when we are discussing the problems that arise with respect to the question of sharing revenues. In my opinion, prior to this kind of legislation, if it cannot be done in the midst of it, if I may put it that way, a dominion-provincial conference should have been called not so much for the purpose of finding a method or a formula to meet the immediate problem of how to share the revenues of the country but rather a constitutional conference. I will grant that an attempt was made not so many years ago to have that kind of conference. Unfortunately, for one reason or another it did not go very far and was not resumed. But I think it is even more important in the long pull, if we are to operate our federal system efficiently, to have a constitutional conference of the provinces with the federal officials and take a good, cool look at the provisions of the British North America Act with the amendments that have been made.
I say that because a great many of these petty and sometimes partisan arguments that come up in a debate of this kind could be avoided if the fields of endeavour, responsibility and jurisdiction were more clearly defined than has been the case up to this time. Certainly we would avoid the one thing which has been deplored by speakers on both sides of the house, and that is the question of one government raising the revenue and another government spending the revenue. Personally I do not think it is the worst thing that could happen in a country, particularly a country like Canada, but it is an undesirable way in which to handle our revenues.

If there were a constitutional conference, and if those who participated took a good look at things, had expert advice, decided what from now on could be more efficiently handled on the provincial level and what in the national interest could be more efficiently handled on the federal level, and then suggested to parliament and eventually to the parliament of Westminster further amendments to our constitution based upon the results of that conference and arising out of commop agreement among the representatives of the provinces and the dominion, we would do away with a great many of the difficulties that arise at a time when we are wondering how best to share these revenues.

speechtext: Is that not what the Rowell-Sirois commission did?

The Minister of Finance asks if that is not what the Rowell-Sirois commission did. I do not quite agree with him that that is what the commission did, if that is the view he holds. What the commission did was to investigate, do a good deal of necessary basic research work and get a great many facts and place them before the government or parliament. The commission's duty was not to propose definite constitutional amendments. They could make certain general recommendations, which they did. They also supplied the background material upon which such decisions can be based, but only the elected representatives of the people can go to the extent of actually recommending the necessary amendments which have to be made to the constitution.
I believe that until we have a conference which will devote itself much more fully and deeply to the question of our constitutional relationships, many of these problems are going to arise again and again. I think what is also required are conferences within the provinces between the municipalities and the provinces themselves. Certainly after such a constitutional conference as I have mentioned had been held; after there had been some clarification and the best possible job had been done within the terms of the agreement among those participating so the provincial jurisdictions knew exactly what their responsibilities were, the provinces would then be in a position to call in the officials of the municipalities within the provinces. Then they could decide in conference to what extent certain changes would have to be made in their various municipal acts and other legislation dealing with municipalities. That should be done in order that there might be some clear-cut idea in the minds of those who are serving the same taxpayer on the municipal, provincial and federal levels.

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements
I think the very worst thing that could happen, and during this debate it has almost happened, would be a competition in passing the buck or trying to make good fellows of ourselves by saying, as the Minister of Fisheries did, "Well, here we are and we are offering you $115 million more." What business have we to offer anything to anybody? Whether members of this federal parliament or of a legislature or of a municipal council we are trustees, and very temporary trustees at that, of certain moneys which are given to us by the people of the country who trust our wisdom to the extent that they feel we will spend those moneys in the best possible interests of all the people concerned. But for the federal government to take the attitude that it has certain moneys which it is in a position to give or grant or hand to any province is, I think, looking at the matter from the wrong point of view.
That is why I suggest there should be some clear-cut arrangements made in order that the various levels of government will know exactly what are their responsibilities. It is quite conceivable that as to many of the things which today are considered to be, and are in the legal sense, the responsibility of the provinces, the time may now have arrived when the provinces themselves will agree that those responsibilities should be transferred to the federal jurisdiction. Having done that piecemeal in a great many respects already, it may perhaps be felt that certain of .the responsibilities should now more properly lie within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. But let there be a clear understanding of those terms and arrangements before we begin to talk actual money.
I want to add this. I believe I should say this because in a sense it has a bearing on this very legislation that we are now discussing. There are certain things this parliament can do to ease the burden on certain parts of this nation which have been referred to as not as well developed as or retarded in relation to other areas. We have to take a good look at our tariff structure. Certainly no one will deny that our tariff structure right from the beginning, its setting up, has had the effect of concentrating industry in certain parts of our nation, which has had the result of asking the people of other provinces which are not favoured by such industry actually to subsidize this industry in the form of higher prices because those industries enjoy that certain protection. That is one of the things this parliament could do without in any way disturbing the autonomy of any province and without in any way having to amend the constitution.
TMr. Zaplitny.]

By reducing our tariff duties on certain products we could come materially to the help of many of those provinces which today find themselves in an inferior position financially.
Those are some of the things that could be done. I think most of all we in this parliament must somehow train ourselves to understand that we are here not as federal representatives as such but rather that we are here as representatives of the same taxpayers who are represented by the members in the provincial legislatures and in the various municipal councils. We should therefore try not to approach these jurisdictions on a competitive basis or on the basis of saying "We can do better than you can".
Let the taxpayer decide who can spend his money most efficiently. Let those who are in the various levels of government lay before the taxpayers in clear terms what in their opinion should be the responsibility of each level of government. Let us approach the whole question from a national point of view so that the people across the country will feel that we do not have a bunch of politicians at the top scrapping amongst themselves for the credit for what is done. Rather let them feel that they are willing so to apportion the revenues of the nation so that each government at every level will have the opportunity to discharge its responsibilities.
Because it is in the position of having access to the greatest volume of revenue of all, I think this parliament should lean over backward to avoid making the provincial governments feel as though they are getting a handout, or as though they are being put on the spot by having a piece of legislation thrown at them on a take it or leave it basis. I think the provincial governments should be made to feel that we are willing to sit down as mature people and say, "Here is a nation with a federal system. There are certain revenues that must be raised. Let us find out what is the best way of doing it so that each level of government may discharge its constitutional responsibilities".

Mr. Speaker, in discussing this bill this house is dealing with what is undoubtedly one of the most difficult problems before the dominion parliament and indeed before the nation as a whole, namely the problem of so adjusting the financial relations between the dominion and the provinces that each governmental authority may be enabled to discharge the responsibilities which are placed upon it.
Before coming to some of the details I desire to discuss tonight I should like to make a suggestion, and I do this in all seriousness. In my opinion one of the reasons there has

been so little progress made in solving this problem-and here I am not wishing to overlook real progress where it has been made- or one of the reasons I do not think we have yet set out our feet firmly on the path of an over-all solution, is that we are trying to fit dominion-provincial relations and the problems of the fiscal relationship between the governments into the strait-jacket of preconceived financial proposals and then cutting the limbs-the arms and the legs- of the various governments in order to fit that garment which has been tailored in the workshop of Harris and company-
Harris tweed.

-instead of measuring the customer and finding out what are his real requirements in the year 1956 and the next 20, 50 or 100 years. I do not think one can go too far in matters of this kind. I have been told not only by this minister but by other ministers, and I am going to take their word for it, that you can explain figures in any way you like, that you can use statistics at your own pleasure. If you want to refer to statistics in respect of unemployment insurance there are two sets of statistics, one which suits the unions and one which suits the government. We have two sets here, one that suits the Minister of Fisheries and one that suits the Minister of National Revenue. Then farther down in the sessional paper we have an asterisk followed by these words:
Customs duties and excise taxes on imports are not included as such figures are available only by port of entry which is no indication of the point of consumption.
I would say that is quite an omission, especially when one considers that British Columbia has approximately one-tenth of the population of the country and that the total

amount of customs duties collected, as indicated in the report, was some $427 million. In other words it is a simple matter to say that you cannot decide who the consumers are in this case, but certainly when you are estimating something it is just as simple to say that as one-tenth of the population is in British Columbia therefore one-tenth of the $427 million is a fair estimate of what would be consumed by the people of that province. Therefore the federal government must have received about $42,750,000 in customs duties which are not shown on this paper. I do not know why the amount is not shown here and why the figures are shown in the fashion they are. I am disturbed to think that our sessional papers should conveniently not show some of these things.
Added to the other discrepancy of $51,925,000, that makes a total of $94,675,000. Just by way of interpolation, I notice that the Minister of Finance looks quite unhappy. I am sure he would have liked to finish this bill this evening and I can feel for him, but he should learn to silence the Minister of Fisheries. That is one of the problems of the house. If he and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration would keep a little quieter possibly it would have its effect on some others of us.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the best speech in this debate was made by the Minister of Fisheries.

The Minister of Fisheries drew attention to certain other factors when referring to the sessional paper, but he failed to point out to the house that customs duties were not taken into account, and I am satisfied that the Minister of Finance, being the fair minister he is, will agree that possibly the Minister of Fisheries was in error in that particular.

With respect to what the minister had to say and having to do with the error, I suggest that the minister was in error in not pointing out to the house that the sessional paper had the specific note:
Customs duties and excise taxes on imports are not included as such figures are available only by port of entry which is no indication of the point of consumption.
He did not read that part of it to the house.
A little matter of $42 million is not much.
You say that $115 million is niggardly.

I go to another item, expenditures by the federal government in the province. Section C refers to interest paid on government of Canada bonds based on the original distribution, by provinces, of the ninth victory loan bond issue. That depends on the interpretation one wants to put on it. Here is a matter of $36,195,000. I am satisfied that the minister would agree that this is an expenditure by the federal government in the province and not a payment to the province; therefore I do not think the impression should be left that the province got something. I would say that a big share of that money is being received by the banks in the community. It is true that a good portion of that amount will be made available through loans and so on, but at the present time the provincial government does not get it and it is not a gain to the province.
I did not say it was.
No, I realize you did not. You did not mention that figure at all.
It is a payment in the province of British Columbia, not to the provincial government.
Very true. I agree with you, but when the banks in the locality have an accumulation of the bonds I am satisfied that they find their way in due course to the central bank.
The people's savings in the banks buy these bonds.

This is not savings. It is government bonds and in all likelihood they were sold to the banks. I know just as well as

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements the minister does that there are thousands of people who did have these bonds. I know there are many thousands of them who bought them originally with the intention of keeping them as long as possible, in the same way as the minister and other members of the house did, but these people have been forced to sell them to the banks because they needed some ready cash, so they are in the hands of the banks today.
But when the banks buy them they buy them with the savings of the people who put their deposits in the banks, so the people own these things indirectly.
And the federal government taxes it away from them.
Who is making this speech, anyway?

With all this assistance I am sure the house will recognize that we are getting somewhere or nowhere, as the case may be. However, it is interesting to note that with that amount added we have a total amount of $130,870,000. I am not satisfied with the minister's interpretation that the people in the province have that money completely in their hands, because I feel it is in the hands of the banks. I know that where money is in the hands of the banks I have a great deal of difficulty in getting my hands on it.
Now you are talking like a C.C.F.'er.

Maybe the minister has hopes that I will lean to the C.C.F., but I assure him that will not be the case.
Mr. Speaker, if we add that $130,870,000 to the reported figure given to the province, namely the sum of $270,857,000 which the minister quotes, it will make a grand total of $401,727,000. Against that the minister has said that the government expended $355 million, from which I would take that $36 million, so that we in the province of British Columbia actually are receiving only about $320 million as compared with the total amount we have given to the federal government of some $401 million.
You had better send those figures to the Auditor General.
We would not send them to you, anyway.

On page 2 of this same report we find this; and I am particularly interested in page 2 because in the past two sessions of this parliament I have tried to arrive at some figure that the government would present me with having to do with the amount that


is expended in the province of British Columbia in the way of defence production. I am pleased to note in section D of this report, "Estimate of major expenditures by government departments or agencies within the province", subsection (d), "Defence production, $221,000." Here are one-tenth of the people of the country and they receive the tremendous sum of $221,000 out of our total defence production expenditures, according to the estimate as set down here. I am pleased that this order for return gives us in British Columbia an idea of what we might expect will be spent in that province.
I could not get the figures.

You could not, I could not nor could anyone else because it was not desirable to indicate them at that time. We have set down in the same section, or rather in subsection (j), as far as national defence is concerned in British Columbia, $92,222,000. That is a substantial increase. But, Mr. Speaker, I think everyone will recognize the fact that a national defence expenditure is not an expenditure for the province of British Columbia alone. It is an expenditure that is intended for the over-all defence of Canada like any other training that we might feel would be necessary. In all fairness I do not think this expenditure of $92,222,000 should have been included as an estimate of major expenditure by governmental departments within the province. It is expended within the province. But even if we assume the suggestion is correct that we receive the expenditure in the province-that is for troops and so on who get it-it does not help in the building of the province in the same way as, let us say, defence production.
In any event, $92,222,000 out of the $1| billion the minister said we expend on our defence program-he indicated earlier, I am sure, that $lf billion is our over-all expenditure; I think that was the figure for defence expenditure estimates, at least-is only one-twentieth Canada's total defence expenditure. If we are going to carry on and recognize that equalization of taxes is a good thing-and I agree that it is a good thing- certainly we should have some semblance of agreement on it. I would say that it is not being carried out in any reasonable way, especially when one stops to consider the vulnerability of the west coast province to attack from those whom we suppose to be our enemies.
The minister said "Where is the money coming from?" He said, "Are we going to increase federal taxes?" I would say to the minister, "No, there is no need to increase federal taxes". I should like to make a suggestion to him, because he has such an

optimistic Minister of Trade and Commerce who continually tells us that the gross national product is going to expand. I should like to suggest that there is no need to increase taxes because your taxes are bound to increase every year as your gross national product expands. Hence the Minister of Finance will not have any trouble at all in finding this money. He just must keep the gross national product increasing. Then on your tax basis, or on the basis as it is today, you will receive more in taxes.
I see the minister shaking his head. I do not mean the Minister of Finance; I mean the Minister of Fisheries. From the negative shake of his head am I to understand that he does not agree with me when I say that if the gross national product increases, the Minister of Finance will get more revenue?
That is when we cut taxes for the Canadian taxpayer, something that is very popular.

Oh, yes; probably we will have that next year for election purposes. But at the same time I am satisfied that this government could make themselves just as popular if they were to help the municipalities and the provincial governments a little bit more. I am particularly interested in the municipalities in an indirect way, through the provincial governments.
